async def connect(self) -> None:
    """Connect to the database by creating the async engine."""
    if self._engine is None:
        engine_options = (
            {**self._options, "isolation_level": "AUTOCOMMIT"}
            if self._autocommit_by_default
            else self._options
        )
        self._engine = create_async_engine(self._url, **engine_options)
        # Engine (or a view of the same engine/pool) in AUTOCOMMIT mode.
        # Standalone queries use this to avoid a BEGIN/COMMIT round-trip
        # per call, matching legacy `databases`-library semantics. Explicit
        # Transactions keep using ``self._engine`` so BEGIN / SAVEPOINT
        # still work.
        self._autocommit_engine = (
            self._engine
            if self._autocommit_by_default
            else self._engine.execution_options(isolation_level="AUTOCOMMIT")
        )

        self.native_backend = build_native_backend(
            dialect=self._engine.dialect, enabled=self._native_execution
        )

        # Set up SQLite foreign keys pragma if using SQLite
        if self._engine.dialect.name == "sqlite":  # pragma: nocover

            @event.listens_for(self._engine.sync_engine, "connect")
            def set_sqlite_pragma(dbapi_conn: Any, connection_record: Any) -> None:
                cursor = dbapi_conn.cursor()
                cursor.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON")
                cursor.close()

        await self._open_min_connections()

        if self._force_rollback:
            assert self._global_transaction is None
            self._global_transaction = Transaction(
                self, force_rollback=self._force_rollback
            )
            await self._global_transaction.__aenter__()

async def disconnect(self) -> None:
    """
    Disconnect from the database and dispose of the engine.
    In case of force_rollback, also roll back the global transaction.
    """
    if self._engine is not None:
        if self._force_rollback:
            assert self._global_transaction is not None
            await self._global_transaction.__aexit__()
            self._global_transaction = None

        await self._engine.dispose()
        self._engine = None
        self._autocommit_engine = None
        self.native_backend = None

async def restore_transaction_isolation(self, conn: AsyncConnection) -> None:
    """
    Switch a freshly checked out connection to the server's default isolation
    level when the engine runs in AUTOCOMMIT, so explicit transactions get
    a real BEGIN / COMMIT. The pool resets it back to AUTOCOMMIT on checkin.

    :param conn: connection checked out from the main engine
    :type conn: AsyncConnection
    """
    if self._autocommit_by_default:  # pragma: no cover
        await conn.execution_options(
            isolation_level=conn.dialect.default_isolation_level
        )

def build_native_backend(dialect: Dialect, enabled: bool) -> Optional[NativeBackend]:
    """
    Build the native backend for the dialect's driver.

    :param dialect: dialect of the connected database
    :type dialect: Dialect
    :param enabled: whether native execution is enabled
    :type enabled: bool
    :return: native backend, or None when disabled or the driver has no adapter
    :rtype: Optional[NativeBackend]
    """
    adapter = select_adapter(dialect=dialect) if enabled else None
    if adapter is None:
        return None
    return NativeBackend(
        dialect=dialect, adapter=adapter, compiler=NativeCompiler(dialect=dialect)
    )

docs.title: QueryExecutor

Executes database queries. With a native backend, statements run directly on the driver connection underneath the SQLAlchemy connection; statements the backend cannot run (and every statement without a backend) go through the SQLAlchemy async API. Provides a databases-compatible interface.

Source code in ormar/databases/query_executor.py Python
class QueryExecutor:
    """
    Executes database queries. With a native backend, statements run directly on
    the driver connection underneath the SQLAlchemy connection; statements the
    backend cannot run (and every statement without a backend) go through the
    SQLAlchemy async API. Provides a databases-compatible interface.
    """

    def __init__(
        self, connection: AsyncConnection, native: Optional[NativeBackend] = None
    ) -> None:
        """
        Initialize query executor.

        :param connection: SQLAlchemy async connection
        :param native: native backend of the database, if the driver has one
        """
        self._connection = connection
        self._native = native
        self._raw: Any = None

    async def fetch_all(
        self, query: Executable, params: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None
    ) -> List[Any]:
        """
        Execute a query and fetch all rows.

        :param query: SQLAlchemy query expression
        :param params: values for named bind parameters of the query, by name;
            a cached query template passes its slot values here
        :return: List of rows, accessible by result label
        """
        bound = self._bind(query=query, params=params)
        if bound is not None:
            return await self._fetch_native(bound=bound)
        result: CursorResult[Any] = await self._connection.execute(
            statement=query, parameters=params
        )
        return list(result.mappings().all())

    async def fetch_one(
        self, query: Executable, params: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None
    ) -> Optional[Mapping[Any, Any]]:
        """
        Execute a query and fetch one row.

        :param query: SQLAlchemy query expression
        :param params: values for named bind parameters of the query, by name;
            a cached query template passes its slot values here
        :return: Single row or None
        """
        bound = self._bind(query=query, params=params)
        if bound is not None:
            rows = await self._fetch_native(bound=bound)
            return rows[0] if rows else None
        result: CursorResult[Any] = await self._connection.execute(
            statement=query, parameters=params
        )
        row = result.mappings().first()
        return row

    async def fetch_val(
        self,
        query: Executable,
        column: int = 0,
        params: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None,
    ) -> Optional[Any]:
        """
        Execute a query and fetch a single scalar value.

        :param query: SQLAlchemy query expression
        :param column: Column index to fetch (default 0)
        :param params: values for named bind parameters of the query, by name;
            a cached query template passes its slot values here
        :return: Scalar value or None
        """
        bound = self._bind(query=query, params=params)
        if bound is not None:
            rows = await self._fetch_native(bound=bound)
            return list(rows[0].values())[column] if rows else None
        result: CursorResult[Any] = await self._connection.execute(
            statement=query, parameters=params
        )
        return result.scalar()

    async def execute(
        self, query: Executable, params: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None
    ) -> Any:
        """
        Execute a query (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE).

        :param query: SQLAlchemy query expression
        :param params: values for named bind parameters of the query
        :return: For INSERT, the inserted primary key or ``None`` if the backend
            cannot return one (e.g. Oracle MySQL inserting into a
            non-AUTO_INCREMENT pk with a server default — no RETURNING support).
            For UPDATE/DELETE, the row count.
        """
        bound = self._bind(query=query, params=params)
        if bound is not None:
            assert self._native is not None
            return await self._run(
                method=self._native.adapter.execute, payload=bound, args=bound.args
            )

        result: CursorResult[Any] = await self._connection.execute(
            statement=query, parameters=params
        )

        # For INSERT queries, try to get the inserted primary key via the
        # dialect's best-available mechanism (RETURNING on PostgreSQL / SQLite
        # 3.35+ / MariaDB 10.5+, LAST_INSERT_ID() on MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT).
        # Do NOT fall back to rowcount here: rowcount is not a pk, and
        # returning it would silently corrupt `Model.pk` in `save()`.
        if result.context and result.context.isinsert:
            # a primary key bound by name (insert templates bind it as
            # ``ormar_v{i}``) is returned as bound: SQLAlchemy only looks the
            # inserted key up under the column key, so it would miss it
            compiled = cast(SQLCompiler, result.context.compiled)
            key = pk_param_key(compiled=compiled) if params else None
            if key is not None and params and params.get(key) is not None:
                return params[key]
            if result.inserted_primary_key:
                pk_value = result.inserted_primary_key[0]
                if pk_value is not None:
                    return pk_value

            if hasattr(result, "lastrowid") and result.lastrowid:  # pragma: no cover
                return result.lastrowid

            return None  # pragma: no cover

        return result.rowcount if result.rowcount is not None else 0

    async def execute_many(
        self, query: Union[Executable, str], values: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]]
    ) -> None:
        """
        Execute a query multiple times with different parameter sets.

        :param query: SQLAlchemy query expression or SQL string
        :param values: Sequence of parameter mappings
        """
        # SQLAlchemy runs a statement given no parameter sets once; leave
        # that case to it so both paths behave the same.
        if self._native is not None and values and is_plannable(stmt=query):
            batch = self._native.compiler.bind_many(stmt=query, rows=values)
            if not batch.plan.fallback:
                await self._run(
                    method=self._native.adapter.execute_many,
                    payload=batch,
                    args=batch.args_list,
                )
                return
        exec_query = text(text=query) if isinstance(query, str) else query
        await self._connection.execute(statement=exec_query, parameters=values)

    async def iterate(
        self, query: Executable, params: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None
    ) -> AsyncIterator[Any]:
        """
        Execute a query and iterate over results.

        :param query: SQLAlchemy query expression
        :param params: values for named bind parameters of the query, by name;
            a cached query template passes its slot values here
        :return: Async iterator of rows, accessible by result label
        """
        bound = self._bind(query=query, params=params)
        if bound is not None:
            assert self._native is not None
            raw = await self._raw_connection()
            rows = self._native.adapter.stream(
                raw=raw, bound=bound, batch_size=ITERATE_BATCH_SIZE
            )
            async with contextlib.aclosing(rows):
                try:
                    async for row in rows:
                        yield row
                except self._native.adapter.driver_errors as error:
                    await self._translate(error=error, sql=bound.sql, args=bound.args)
                except GeneratorExit:
                    raise
                except BaseException as error:
                    await self._reraise_interrupted(error=error)
            return
        async with self._connection.stream(
            statement=query, parameters=params
        ) as result:
            async for mapping in result.mappings():
                yield mapping

    async def _fetch_native(self, bound: BoundStatement) -> List[Any]:
        """
        Fetch all rows of a bound statement on the driver.

        :param bound: bound statement
        :return: rows keyed by result label
        """
        assert self._native is not None
        return await self._run(
            method=self._native.adapter.fetch_all, payload=bound, args=bound.args
        )

    def _bind(
        self, query: Executable, params: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None
    ) -> Optional[BoundStatement]:
        """
        Bind the query for native execution.

        :param query: SQLAlchemy query expression
        :param params: values for named bind parameters of the query, by name;
            a cached query template passes its slot values here
        :return: bound statement, or None when it must run through SQLAlchemy
        """
        if self._native is None or not is_plannable(stmt=query):
            return None
        bound = self._native.compiler.bind(stmt=query, params=params)
        return None if bound.plan.fallback else bound

    async def _raw_connection(self) -> Any:
        """
        Return the pooled raw connection under the SQLAlchemy connection.

        :return: pooled raw connection
        """
        if self._raw is None:
            # an established connection already holds its pooled connection;
            # only a lazy, not yet connected one needs SQLAlchemy's greenlet
            sync_connection = self._connection.sync_connection
            if sync_connection is not None and (
                sync_connection._dbapi_connection is not None
            ):
                self._raw = sync_connection._dbapi_connection
            else:
                self._raw = await self._connection.get_raw_connection()
        return self._raw

    async def _run(
        self,
        method: Callable[[Any, Payload], Awaitable[Result]],
        payload: Payload,
        args: Sequence[Any],
    ) -> Result:
        """
        Run an adapter method, translating driver errors to SQLAlchemy ones.

        :param method: adapter method to run
        :param payload: bound statement or batch
        :param args: driver arguments, reported in a translated error
        :return: result of the adapter method
        """
        assert self._native is not None
        raw = await self._raw_connection()
        try:
            return await method(raw, payload)
        except self._native.adapter.driver_errors as error:
            await self._translate(
                error=error,
                sql=payload.sql,
                args=args,
                ismulti=isinstance(payload, BoundBatch),
            )
        except BaseException as error:
            await self._reraise_interrupted(error=error)

    async def _reraise_interrupted(self, error: BaseException) -> NoReturn:
        """
        Re-raise an exception from a native call, first invalidating the
        connection when the call was interrupted (task cancellation,
        KeyboardInterrupt, ...), as SQLAlchemy does, so a connection left
        mid-statement never returns to the pool.

        :param error: exception raised during the call
        """
        if util.is_exit_exception(e=error):
            await self._connection.invalidate()
        raise error

    async def _translate(
        self,
        error: BaseException,
        sql: str,
        args: Sequence[Any],
        ismulti: bool = False,
    ) -> NoReturn:
        """
        Re-raise a driver error as the matching SQLAlchemy exception.

        :param error: exception raised by the driver
        :param sql: executed SQL
        :param args: driver arguments
        :param ismulti: whether the statement ran once per row of a batch
        """
        assert self._native is not None
        await raise_translated(
            error=error,
            backend=self._native,
            sa_connection=self._connection,
            sql=sql,
            args=args,
            ismulti=ismulti,
        )

async def execute(
    self, query: Executable, params: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None
) -> Any:
    """
    Execute a query (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE).

    :param query: SQLAlchemy query expression
    :param params: values for named bind parameters of the query
    :return: For INSERT, the inserted primary key or ``None`` if the backend
        cannot return one (e.g. Oracle MySQL inserting into a
        non-AUTO_INCREMENT pk with a server default — no RETURNING support).
        For UPDATE/DELETE, the row count.
    """
    bound = self._bind(query=query, params=params)
    if bound is not None:
        assert self._native is not None
        return await self._run(
            method=self._native.adapter.execute, payload=bound, args=bound.args
        )

    result: CursorResult[Any] = await self._connection.execute(
        statement=query, parameters=params
    )

    # For INSERT queries, try to get the inserted primary key via the
    # dialect's best-available mechanism (RETURNING on PostgreSQL / SQLite
    # 3.35+ / MariaDB 10.5+, LAST_INSERT_ID() on MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT).
    # Do NOT fall back to rowcount here: rowcount is not a pk, and
    # returning it would silently corrupt `Model.pk` in `save()`.
    if result.context and result.context.isinsert:
        # a primary key bound by name (insert templates bind it as
        # ``ormar_v{i}``) is returned as bound: SQLAlchemy only looks the
        # inserted key up under the column key, so it would miss it
        compiled = cast(SQLCompiler, result.context.compiled)
        key = pk_param_key(compiled=compiled) if params else None
        if key is not None and params and params.get(key) is not None:
            return params[key]
        if result.inserted_primary_key:
            pk_value = result.inserted_primary_key[0]
            if pk_value is not None:
                return pk_value

        if hasattr(result, "lastrowid") and result.lastrowid:  # pragma: no cover
            return result.lastrowid

        return None  # pragma: no cover

    return result.rowcount if result.rowcount is not None else 0

async def execute_many(
    self, query: Union[Executable, str], values: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]]
) -> None:
    """
    Execute a query multiple times with different parameter sets.

    :param query: SQLAlchemy query expression or SQL string
    :param values: Sequence of parameter mappings
    """
    # SQLAlchemy runs a statement given no parameter sets once; leave
    # that case to it so both paths behave the same.
    if self._native is not None and values and is_plannable(stmt=query):
        batch = self._native.compiler.bind_many(stmt=query, rows=values)
        if not batch.plan.fallback:
            await self._run(
                method=self._native.adapter.execute_many,
                payload=batch,
                args=batch.args_list,
            )
            return
    exec_query = text(text=query) if isinstance(query, str) else query
    await self._connection.execute(statement=exec_query, parameters=values)

async def iterate(
    self, query: Executable, params: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None
) -> AsyncIterator[Any]:
    """
    Execute a query and iterate over results.

    :param query: SQLAlchemy query expression
    :param params: values for named bind parameters of the query, by name;
        a cached query template passes its slot values here
    :return: Async iterator of rows, accessible by result label
    """
    bound = self._bind(query=query, params=params)
    if bound is not None:
        assert self._native is not None
        raw = await self._raw_connection()
        rows = self._native.adapter.stream(
            raw=raw, bound=bound, batch_size=ITERATE_BATCH_SIZE
        )
        async with contextlib.aclosing(rows):
            try:
                async for row in rows:
                    yield row
            except self._native.adapter.driver_errors as error:
                await self._translate(error=error, sql=bound.sql, args=bound.args)
            except GeneratorExit:
                raise
            except BaseException as error:
                await self._reraise_interrupted(error=error)
        return
    async with self._connection.stream(
        statement=query, parameters=params
    ) as result:
        async for mapping in result.mappings():
            yield mapping

class Transaction:
    """
    Transaction context manager with support for nested transactions via savepoints.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        database: "DatabaseConnection",
        force_rollback: bool = False,
    ) -> None:
        """
        Initialize transaction.

        :param database: DatabaseConnection instance
        :param force_rollback: If True, always rollback (used for testing)
        """
        self._database = database
        self._force_rollback = force_rollback
        self._connection: Optional[AsyncConnection] = None
        self._transaction: Optional[AsyncTransaction] = None
        self._depth: int = 0

    async def __aenter__(self) -> "Transaction":
        """Enter transaction context."""
        self._depth = _transaction_depth.get()

        # If this is the outermost transaction, get a new connection from the
        # main engine, so ``connection.begin()`` and the nested
        # ``begin_nested()`` savepoints below both work.
        if self._depth == 0:
            self._connection = await self._database.engine.connect().__aenter__()
            is_sqlite = self._database.engine.dialect.name == "sqlite"
            # SQLite gets an explicit BEGIN below, which opens a real transaction
            # even on an AUTOCOMMIT connection, so its isolation level stays as is.
            if not is_sqlite:  # pragma: nocover
                await self._database.restore_transaction_isolation(self._connection)
            self._database.set_transaction_connection(self._connection)
            self._transaction = await self._connection.begin()
            # SQLite requires an explicit BEGIN before SAVEPOINTs to prevent
            # RELEASE SAVEPOINT from auto-committing when no outer transaction exists.
            # Issue after conn.begin() to avoid conflicting with SQLAlchemy's autobegin.
            if is_sqlite:  # pragma: nocover
                await self._connection.exec_driver_sql("BEGIN")
            # Natively executed statements bypass SQLAlchemy, whose asyncpg
            # adapter only starts the transaction on its own first statement.
            await self._database.start_driver_transaction(connection=self._connection)
        else:
            # Nested transaction - use savepoint
            self._connection = self._database.get_transaction_connection()
            assert self._connection is not None
            self._transaction = await self._connection.begin_nested()

        _transaction_depth.set(self._depth + 1)

        return self

    async def __aexit__(
        self,
        exc_type: Optional[Type[BaseException]] = None,
        exc_value: Optional[BaseException] = None,
        traceback: Optional[TracebackType] = None,
    ) -> None:
        """Exit transaction context."""
        try:
            _transaction_depth.set(self._depth)

            # Handle transaction completion
            if self._transaction is not None:
                if exc_type is not None or self._force_rollback:
                    await self._transaction.rollback()
                else:
                    await self._transaction.commit()
        finally:
            if self._depth == 0:
                self._database.set_transaction_connection(None)
                if self._connection is not None:
                    await self._connection.close()

docs.title: compiler
docs.text:
Turns SQLAlchemy statements into SQL text plus positional arguments that a native async driver can run directly, skipping SQLAlchemy's execution layer.

SQLAlchemy still builds and compiles every statement; this module reuses its compiled output. A compiled statement holds its SQL with the driver's placeholders and the names of its bind parameters in placeholder order, so running it natively means looking each value up by name in that order::

Text Only
stmt = select(users.c.id, users.c.name).where(users.c.id == 5)
# compiled for asyncpg
sql == "SELECT users.id, users.name FROM users WHERE users.id = $1::INTEGER"
args == [5]  # value of the bind parameter named "id_1"

Compiling is the expensive part, so compiled statements are cached per statement shape and only the values are bound on each call.

class NativeCompiler:
    """
    Turns statements into ``BoundStatement`` / ``BoundBatch`` objects for one
    database dialect.

    Compiling is the costly step, so plans are kept in an LRU cache keyed by
    SQLAlchemy's statement cache key, which is equal for all statements of one
    shape whatever their values. On a hit only the new values are bound::

        compiler.bind(select(users).where(users.c.id == 5))  # compiles
        compiler.bind(select(users).where(users.c.id == 7))  # reuses the plan
    """

    def __init__(self, dialect: Dialect, max_plans: int = 2048) -> None:
        """
        :param dialect: dialect of the database the statements run on
        :type dialect: Dialect
        :param max_plans: number of compiled statement shapes kept in memory
        :type max_plans: int
        """
        self.dialect = dialect
        self.max_plans = max_plans
        self._plans: "OrderedDict[Any, StatementPlan]" = OrderedDict()

    def bind(
        self, stmt: Executable, params: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None
    ) -> BoundStatement:
        """
        Compile the statement, or reuse the plan of its shape, and bind its values
        into SQL and positional driver arguments.

        The values come from the statement's own cache key, which carries the
        bound values of this particular statement::

            bind(select(users.c.id).where(users.c.id == 7))
            # -> sql "... WHERE users.id = $1::INTEGER", args [7]

        ``params`` supplies values by bind name instead. ormar's cached query
        templates use it: one statement built once with named slots, and only
        the values passed on each call::

            stmt = select(users.c.id).where(users.c.id == bindparam("ormar_p0"))
            bind(stmt, {"ormar_p0": 7})  # -> args [7]

        When ``binds_directly`` allows it, those values go to the driver
        without SQLAlchemy's binding steps (see ``direct_args``).

        :param stmt: statement to execute
        :type stmt: Executable
        :param params: values for named bind parameters, by name
        :type params: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]]
        :return: plan, SQL string and positional driver arguments
        :rtype: BoundStatement
        """
        key = stmt._generate_cache_key()  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
        plan = self._plan(stmt=stmt, key=key)
        if params is not None and binds_directly(compiled=plan.compiled, row=params):
            args = direct_args(plan=plan, rows=[params])[0]
            return BoundStatement(
                plan=plan, sql=plan.compiled.string, args=args, params=dict(params)
            )
        bound_params = plan.compiled.construct_params(
            params=params,
            extracted_parameters=key[1] if key is not None else None,
            escape_names=True,
            _no_postcompile=True,
        )
        apply_prefetch_defaults(compiled=plan.compiled, params=bound_params)
        sql, args = expand(compiled=plan.compiled, params=bound_params)
        return BoundStatement(plan=plan, sql=sql, args=args, params=bound_params)

    def bind_many(
        self, stmt: Executable, rows: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]]
    ) -> BoundBatch:
        """
        Compile a statement with named ``bindparam`` placeholders, or reuse its
        plan, and bind one set of values per row for ``executemany``::

            bind_many(users.insert(), [{"name": "a"}, {"name": "b"}])
            # -> sql "INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ($1::VARCHAR)",
            #    args_list [["a"], ["b"]]

        Like ``bind``, rows that ``binds_directly`` accepts skip SQLAlchemy's
        binding steps.

        :param stmt: statement with ``bindparam`` placeholders
        :type stmt: Executable
        :param rows: parameter values per row, keyed by bind parameter name
        :type rows: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]]
        :return: plan, SQL string and positional driver arguments per row
        :rtype: BoundBatch
        """
        key = stmt._generate_cache_key()  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
        plan = self._plan(stmt=stmt, key=key)
        if rows and binds_directly(compiled=plan.compiled, row=rows[0]):
            return BoundBatch(
                plan=plan,
                sql=plan.compiled.string,
                args_list=direct_args(plan=plan, rows=rows),
            )
        sql = ""
        args_list = []
        for row in rows:
            params = plan.compiled.construct_params(
                params=row,
                extracted_parameters=key[1] if key is not None else None,
                escape_names=True,
                _no_postcompile=True,
            )
            apply_prefetch_defaults(compiled=plan.compiled, params=params)
            sql, args = expand(compiled=plan.compiled, params=params)
            args_list.append(args)
        return BoundBatch(plan=plan, sql=sql, args_list=args_list)

    def _plan(self, stmt: Executable, key: Any) -> StatementPlan:
        """
        Return the cached plan for the statement shape, compiling it on a miss.
        Statements SQLAlchemy cannot cache (no cache key) are compiled every time;
        past ``max_plans`` the least recently used plan is dropped.

        :param stmt: statement to plan
        :type stmt: Executable
        :param key: SQLAlchemy cache key of the statement, or None if uncacheable
        :type key: Any
        :return: plan for the statement shape
        :rtype: StatementPlan
        """
        if key is None:
            return self._compile(stmt=stmt, key=key)
        plan = self._plans.get(key.key)
        if plan is not None:
            self._plans.move_to_end(key.key)
            return plan
        plan = self._compile(stmt=stmt, key=key)
        self._plans[key.key] = plan
        if len(self._plans) > self.max_plans:
            self._plans.popitem(last=False)
        return plan

    def _compile(self, stmt: Executable, key: Any) -> StatementPlan:
        """
        Compile the statement for the dialect and derive its plan. Passing the
        cache key makes SQLAlchemy record which bind parameters come from the key,
        so later statements of the same shape can supply their own values.

        :param stmt: statement to compile
        :type stmt: Executable
        :param key: SQLAlchemy cache key of the statement, or None
        :type key: Any
        :return: plan for the statement shape
        :rtype: StatementPlan
        """
        compiled = stmt._compiler(  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
            dialect=self.dialect, cache_key=key
        )
        plan = StatementPlan(compiled=compiled)
        if plan.is_insert:
            plan.pk_param_key = pk_param_key(compiled=compiled)
        return plan

Compile the statement, or reuse the plan of its shape, and bind its values into SQL and positional driver arguments.

The values come from the statement's own cache key, which carries the bound values of this particular statement::

Text Only
bind(select(users.c.id).where(users.c.id == 7))
# -> sql "... WHERE users.id = $1::INTEGER", args [7]

params supplies values by bind name instead. ormar's cached query templates use it: one statement built once with named slots, and only the values passed on each call::

Text Only
stmt = select(users.c.id).where(users.c.id == bindparam("ormar_p0"))
bind(stmt, {"ormar_p0": 7})  # -> args [7]

When binds_directly allows it, those values go to the driver without SQLAlchemy's binding steps (see direct_args).

:param stmt: statement to execute :type stmt: Executable :param params: values for named bind parameters, by name :type params: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] :return: plan, SQL string and positional driver arguments :rtype: BoundStatement

def bind(
    self, stmt: Executable, params: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None
) -> BoundStatement:
    """
    Compile the statement, or reuse the plan of its shape, and bind its values
    into SQL and positional driver arguments.

    The values come from the statement's own cache key, which carries the
    bound values of this particular statement::

        bind(select(users.c.id).where(users.c.id == 7))
        # -> sql "... WHERE users.id = $1::INTEGER", args [7]

    ``params`` supplies values by bind name instead. ormar's cached query
    templates use it: one statement built once with named slots, and only
    the values passed on each call::

        stmt = select(users.c.id).where(users.c.id == bindparam("ormar_p0"))
        bind(stmt, {"ormar_p0": 7})  # -> args [7]

    When ``binds_directly`` allows it, those values go to the driver
    without SQLAlchemy's binding steps (see ``direct_args``).

    :param stmt: statement to execute
    :type stmt: Executable
    :param params: values for named bind parameters, by name
    :type params: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]]
    :return: plan, SQL string and positional driver arguments
    :rtype: BoundStatement
    """
    key = stmt._generate_cache_key()  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
    plan = self._plan(stmt=stmt, key=key)
    if params is not None and binds_directly(compiled=plan.compiled, row=params):
        args = direct_args(plan=plan, rows=[params])[0]
        return BoundStatement(
            plan=plan, sql=plan.compiled.string, args=args, params=dict(params)
        )
    bound_params = plan.compiled.construct_params(
        params=params,
        extracted_parameters=key[1] if key is not None else None,
        escape_names=True,
        _no_postcompile=True,
    )
    apply_prefetch_defaults(compiled=plan.compiled, params=bound_params)
    sql, args = expand(compiled=plan.compiled, params=bound_params)
    return BoundStatement(plan=plan, sql=sql, args=args, params=bound_params)

def bind_many(
    self, stmt: Executable, rows: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]]
) -> BoundBatch:
    """
    Compile a statement with named ``bindparam`` placeholders, or reuse its
    plan, and bind one set of values per row for ``executemany``::

        bind_many(users.insert(), [{"name": "a"}, {"name": "b"}])
        # -> sql "INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ($1::VARCHAR)",
        #    args_list [["a"], ["b"]]

    Like ``bind``, rows that ``binds_directly`` accepts skip SQLAlchemy's
    binding steps.

    :param stmt: statement with ``bindparam`` placeholders
    :type stmt: Executable
    :param rows: parameter values per row, keyed by bind parameter name
    :type rows: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]]
    :return: plan, SQL string and positional driver arguments per row
    :rtype: BoundBatch
    """
    key = stmt._generate_cache_key()  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
    plan = self._plan(stmt=stmt, key=key)
    if rows and binds_directly(compiled=plan.compiled, row=rows[0]):
        return BoundBatch(
            plan=plan,
            sql=plan.compiled.string,
            args_list=direct_args(plan=plan, rows=rows),
        )
    sql = ""
    args_list = []
    for row in rows:
        params = plan.compiled.construct_params(
            params=row,
            extracted_parameters=key[1] if key is not None else None,
            escape_names=True,
            _no_postcompile=True,
        )
        apply_prefetch_defaults(compiled=plan.compiled, params=params)
        sql, args = expand(compiled=plan.compiled, params=params)
        args_list.append(args)
    return BoundBatch(plan=plan, sql=sql, args_list=args_list)

It also accepts the selected column objects as keys, like SQLAlchemy's RowMapping does, so code indexing rows that way keeps working::

Text Only
row = NativeRow({"id": 1, "name": "a"})

Each plan builds its own subclass (row_class_for) whose object_keys maps the selected column objects to their labels.

class NativeRow(dict):
    """
    A result row of native execution: a dict keyed by result label, which is
    how ormar reads rows.

    It also accepts the selected column objects as keys, like SQLAlchemy's
    ``RowMapping`` does, so code indexing rows that way keeps working::

        row = NativeRow({"id": 1, "name": "a"})
        row["name"] == row[users.c.name] == "a"

    Each plan builds its own subclass (``row_class_for``) whose
    ``object_keys`` maps the selected column objects to their labels.
    """

    object_keys: Dict[int, str] = {}

    def __missing__(self, key: Any) -> Any:
        """
        Called by dict lookup when the key is not a label: treat the key as a
        selected column object (``row[users.c.name]``) and return its value.

        :param key: column object (or unknown key)
        :type key: Any
        :raises KeyError: when the key is not a selected column
        :return: value of the matching result column
        :rtype: Any
        """
        label = self.object_keys.get(id(key))
        if label is None:
            raise KeyError(key)
        return self[label]

Everything needed to run one statement shape natively, worked out once when the shape is first compiled and reused by every later execution.

select(users.c.id).where(users.c.id == 5) and the same query with 7 have one shape, so they share one plan; only their bound values differ.

It holds the compiled statement, the result labels and types used to build rows, and fallback: True for statements that must run through SQLAlchemy instead (plain text without result columns, duplicate result labels, or column defaults that have to run in the database first).

class StatementPlan:
    """
    Everything needed to run one statement shape natively, worked out once
    when the shape is first compiled and reused by every later execution.

    ``select(users.c.id).where(users.c.id == 5)`` and the same query with ``7``
    have one shape, so they share one plan; only their bound values differ.

    It holds the compiled statement, the result labels and types used to build
    rows, and ``fallback``: True for statements that must run through
    SQLAlchemy instead (plain text without result columns, duplicate result
    labels, or column defaults that have to run in the database first).
    """

    def __init__(self, compiled: SQLCompiler) -> None:
        """
        Build the plan from a statement compiled with its cache key.

        :param compiled: statement compiled for the target dialect
        :type compiled: SQLCompiler
        """
        self.compiled = compiled
        result_columns = compiled._result_columns or []
        self.result_keys: Tuple[str, ...] = tuple(col[0] for col in result_columns)
        self.result_types: Tuple[Any, ...] = tuple(col[3] for col in result_columns)
        self.result_processors: Optional[List[ResultProcessor]] = None
        self.processed_columns: Tuple[Tuple[str, Callable[[Any], Any]], ...] = ()
        self.row_class = row_class_for(result_columns=result_columns)
        self.returning = bool(compiled.effective_returning)
        self.is_insert = bool(compiled.isinsert)
        self.pk_param_key: Optional[str] = None
        # Native execution needs to know the shape of what it runs: DML, or a
        # statement with known result columns. Plain text and DDL go through
        # SQLAlchemy, as do defaults SQLAlchemy must pre-execute.
        is_dml = compiled.isinsert or compiled.isupdate or compiled.isdelete
        duplicate_labels = len(set(self.result_keys)) != len(self.result_keys)
        self.fallback = (
            not (is_dml or self.result_keys)
            or duplicate_labels
            or any(
                not (default.is_scalar or default.is_callable)
                for default in prefetch_defaults(compiled=compiled)
            )
        )

Constants are copied, callables are called (with a DefaultContext)::

Column("token", String, default=lambda: "tok")
users.insert().values(name="a")
# params {"name": "a"} -> {"name": "a", "token": "tok"}

:param compiled: compiled statement :type compiled: SQLCompiler :param params: bound parameters, updated in place :type params: MutableMapping[str, Any]

def apply_prefetch_defaults(
    compiled: SQLCompiler, params: MutableMapping[str, Any]
) -> None:
    """
    Fill the values of execution-time column defaults into the bound
    parameters, which SQLAlchemy's execution context does on its own path.

    Constants are copied, callables are called (with a ``DefaultContext``)::

        Column("token", String, default=lambda: "tok")
        users.insert().values(name="a")
        # params {"name": "a"} -> {"name": "a", "token": "tok"}

    :param compiled: compiled statement
    :type compiled: SQLCompiler
    :param params: bound parameters, updated in place
    :type params: MutableMapping[str, Any]
    """
    if not (compiled.insert_prefetch or compiled.update_prefetch):
        return
    key_getter = compiled._within_exec_param_key_getter
    for columns, attribute in (
        (compiled.insert_prefetch, "default"),
        (compiled.update_prefetch, "onupdate"),
    ):
        for column in columns:
            default = getattr(column, attribute)
            if default.is_scalar:
                params[key_getter(column)] = default.arg
            elif default.is_callable:
                context = DefaultContext(
                    params=unescaped_view(compiled=compiled, params=params),
                    column=column,
                )
                params[key_getter(column)] = default.arg(context)

docs.title: binds_directly(compiled, row)
docs.text:
Return whether values given by bind name can go to the driver as they are, skipping SQLAlchemy's construct_params and expand.

Binding attaches the values to the placeholders of the compiled SQL. The SQL and the values travel to the driver separately, which keeps values out of the SQL text and lets the database reuse one prepared statement::

Text Only
sql = "SELECT users.id FROM users WHERE users.id = $1"
args = [7]
await driver.fetch(sql, *args)

SQLAlchemy's binding (construct_params plus expand) does five things:

  1. collects the values by bind name, e.g. {"id_1": 7}
  2. fills in column defaults run at execution time (default=)
  3. expands IN lists, rewriting the SQL: IN ($1) with [1, 2, 3] becomes IN ($1, $2, $3)
  4. converts each value with its type's bind processor, e.g. a dict for a JSON column becomes a JSON string on SQLite
  5. orders the values by placeholder position (positiontup): ["name", "id_1"] gives ["a", 1]

Those steps cost more than the query itself for small statements. When steps 2 and 3 have nothing to do and no names are escaped, the compiled SQL is already final and binding is only steps 4 and 5, which direct_args does in one pass with the same result. That is not the case with:

  • IN lists and other post-compile parameters (placeholders added per value) and literal-execute parameters (value rendered into the SQL)
  • column defaults SQLAlchemy fills in at execution time
  • escaped bind names (the row is keyed by the original name)

  • a bind the row does not supply::

    stmt = select(users.c.id).where(users.c.id == bindparam("ormar_p0")) binds_directly(compiled, {"ormar_p0": 7}) # -> True stmt = select(users.c.id).where(users.c.id.in_(bindparam("ormar_p0"))) binds_directly(compiled, {"ormar_p0": [1, 2]}) # -> False

:param compiled: compiled statement :type compiled: SQLCompiler :param row: first row of the batch, keyed by bind parameter name :type row: Mapping[str, Any] :return: True when direct_args produces the driver arguments :rtype: bool

def binds_directly(compiled: SQLCompiler, row: Mapping[str, Any]) -> bool:
    """
    Return whether values given by bind name can go to the driver as they
    are, skipping SQLAlchemy's ``construct_params`` and ``expand``.

    Binding attaches the values to the placeholders of the compiled SQL. The
    SQL and the values travel to the driver separately, which keeps values
    out of the SQL text and lets the database reuse one prepared statement::

        sql = "SELECT users.id FROM users WHERE users.id = $1"
        args = [7]
        await driver.fetch(sql, *args)

    SQLAlchemy's binding (``construct_params`` plus ``expand``) does five
    things:

    1. collects the values by bind name, e.g. ``{"id_1": 7}``
    2. fills in column defaults run at execution time (``default=``)
    3. expands ``IN`` lists, rewriting the SQL: ``IN ($1)`` with ``[1, 2, 3]``
       becomes ``IN ($1, $2, $3)``
    4. converts each value with its type's bind processor, e.g. a dict for a
       JSON column becomes a JSON string on SQLite
    5. orders the values by placeholder position (``positiontup``):
       ``["name", "id_1"]`` gives ``["a", 1]``

    Those steps cost more than the query itself for small statements. When
    steps 2 and 3 have nothing to do and no names are escaped, the compiled
    SQL is already final and binding is only steps 4 and 5, which
    ``direct_args`` does in one pass with the same result. That is not the
    case with:

    - ``IN`` lists and other post-compile parameters (placeholders added per
      value) and literal-execute parameters (value rendered into the SQL)
    - column defaults SQLAlchemy fills in at execution time
    - escaped bind names (the row is keyed by the original name)
    - a bind the row does not supply::

        stmt = select(users.c.id).where(users.c.id == bindparam("ormar_p0"))
        binds_directly(compiled, {"ormar_p0": 7})  # -> True
        stmt = select(users.c.id).where(users.c.id.in_(bindparam("ormar_p0")))
        binds_directly(compiled, {"ormar_p0": [1, 2]})  # -> False

    :param compiled: compiled statement
    :type compiled: SQLCompiler
    :param row: first row of the batch, keyed by bind parameter name
    :type row: Mapping[str, Any]
    :return: True when ``direct_args`` produces the driver arguments
    :rtype: bool
    """
    names = compiled.positiontup
    return (
        names is not None
        and not compiled.post_compile_params
        and not compiled.literal_execute_params
        and not compiled.insert_prefetch
        and not compiled.update_prefetch
        and not compiled.escaped_bind_names
        and all(name in row for name in names)
    )

def direct_args(
    plan: StatementPlan, rows: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]]
) -> List[List[Any]]:
    """
    Build the positional driver arguments of each row straight from its
    values, for statements ``binds_directly`` accepts. Values are taken in
    placeholder order and converted by their bind processors, which gives the
    same arguments as ``construct_params`` plus ``expand``::

        # positiontup ["name", "id_1"], no processors
        direct_args(plan, [{"id_1": 1, "name": "a"}])  # -> [["a", 1]]

    :param plan: plan of the statement
    :type plan: StatementPlan
    :param rows: parameter values per row, keyed by bind parameter name
    :type rows: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]]
    :return: positional arguments per row
    :rtype: List[List[Any]]
    """
    compiled = plan.compiled
    processors: Dict[str, Any] = dict(compiled._bind_processors)
    binds = [(name, processors.get(name)) for name in compiled.positiontup or []]
    return [
        [
            processor(row[name]) if processor is not None else row[name]
            for name, processor in binds
        ]
        for row in rows
    ]

docs.title: expand(compiled, params)
docs.text:
Produce the final SQL and positional driver arguments from named parameters.

SQLAlchemy lists the bind names in placeholder order (positiontup), so the arguments are the values looked up in that order. Each value goes through its type's bind processor when it has one, the reverse of a result processor (e.g. a dict to a JSON string on SQLite). IN lists get one placeholder per value::

Text Only
{"id_1": [1, 2, 3]}
# -> "... WHERE users.id IN ($1::INTEGER, $2::INTEGER, $3::INTEGER)",
#    [1, 2, 3]

:param compiled: compiled statement :type compiled: SQLCompiler :param params: bound parameters :type params: MutableMapping[str, Any] :return: SQL string and positional arguments :rtype: Tuple[str, List[Any]]

Source code in ormar/databases/native/compiler.py Python
def expand(
    compiled: SQLCompiler, params: MutableMapping[str, Any]
) -> Tuple[str, List[Any]]:
    """
    Produce the final SQL and positional driver arguments from named
    parameters.

    SQLAlchemy lists the bind names in placeholder order (``positiontup``), so
    the arguments are the values looked up in that order. Each value goes
    through its type's bind processor when it has one, the reverse of a result
    processor (e.g. a dict to a JSON string on SQLite). ``IN`` lists get one
    placeholder per value::

        {"id_1": [1, 2, 3]}
        # -> "... WHERE users.id IN ($1::INTEGER, $2::INTEGER, $3::INTEGER)",
        #    [1, 2, 3]

    :param compiled: compiled statement
    :type compiled: SQLCompiler
    :param params: bound parameters
    :type params: MutableMapping[str, Any]
    :return: SQL string and positional arguments
    :rtype: Tuple[str, List[Any]]
    """
    expanded = compiled.construct_expanded_state(params=params, escape_names=False)
    processors: Dict[str, Any] = {
        **compiled._bind_processors,
        **expanded.processors,
    }
    values = expanded.parameters
    args = [
        processors[name](values[name]) if name in processors else values[name]
        for name in expanded.positiontup or []
    ]
    return expanded.statement, args

def pk_param_key(compiled: SQLCompiler) -> Optional[str]:
    """
    Return the parameter name the INSERT binds the primary key under, or None
    when the INSERT does not set it.

    A primary key provided by the caller is returned as the inserted key
    instead of asking the database, which cannot always report it::

        users.insert().values(id=3, name="a")  # -> "id"
        users.insert().values(name="a")  # -> None

    ormar's cached INSERT templates bind the primary key under their own
    parameter name, which is returned instead of the column key::

        users.insert().values(id=bindparam("ormar_id"))  # -> "ormar_id"

    :param compiled: compiled insert statement
    :type compiled: SQLCompiler
    :return: bind parameter key of the primary key, or None
    :rtype: Optional[str]
    """
    table = compiled.statement.table  # type: ignore[union-attr]
    primary_key = list(table.primary_key.columns)
    if len(primary_key) != 1:  # pragma: no cover
        return None
    values = getattr(compiled.statement, "_values", None) or {}
    for column, value in values.items():
        column_key = column if isinstance(column, str) else column.key
        named_bind = isinstance(value, BindParameter) and not value.unique
        if column_key == primary_key[0].key and named_bind:
            return str(value.key)
    key = compiled._within_exec_param_key_getter(primary_key[0])
    return key if key in compiled.binds else None

docs.text:
Return the column defaults SQLAlchemy fills in at execution time because the statement does not set those columns itself.

SQLAlchemy calls these columns "prefetch": insert_prefetch for default= on INSERT and update_prefetch for onupdate= on UPDATE::

Text Only
Column("token", String, default=lambda: "tok")
users.insert().values(name="a")  # -> [CallableColumnDefault(<lambda>)]

StatementPlan falls back to SQLAlchemy when one of them is neither a constant nor a Python callable (a SQL expression run before the statement).

:param compiled: compiled statement :type compiled: SQLCompiler :return: column defaults (or onupdates) of prefetched columns :rtype: List[Any]

def prefetch_defaults(compiled: SQLCompiler) -> List[Any]:
    """
    Return the column defaults SQLAlchemy fills in at execution time because
    the statement does not set those columns itself.

    SQLAlchemy calls these columns "prefetch": ``insert_prefetch`` for
    ``default=`` on INSERT and ``update_prefetch`` for ``onupdate=`` on
    UPDATE::

        Column("token", String, default=lambda: "tok")
        users.insert().values(name="a")  # -> [CallableColumnDefault(<lambda>)]

    ``StatementPlan`` falls back to SQLAlchemy when one of them is neither a
    constant nor a Python callable (a SQL expression run before the statement).

    :param compiled: compiled statement
    :type compiled: SQLCompiler
    :return: column defaults (or onupdates) of prefetched columns
    :rtype: List[Any]
    """
    defaults = [col.default for col in compiled.insert_prefetch]
    defaults.extend(col.onupdate for col in compiled.update_prefetch)
    return [default for default in defaults if default is not None]

docs.title: resolve_result_processors(plan, dialect, coltypes)
docs.text:
Look up, once per plan, the result processor of each result column.

A result processor is the function a SQLAlchemy type uses to turn the raw value a driver returns into the Python value of that type. Drivers return what the database stores, which is not always what the column type promises, e.g. on SQLite::

Text Only
DateTime  "2024-01-02 03:04:05" -> datetime(2024, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
JSON      '{"a": 1}'            -> {"a": 1}
Enum(C)   "red"                 -> C.red
Boolean   1                     -> True
Integer   needs none            -> None

SQLAlchemy runs them on its own path; the native path must run the same ones, or rows would hold driver values. Some types pick their processor by the column type the driver reports (a PostgreSQL NUMERIC read into a Numeric(asdecimal=False) column needs a float conversion), so this runs on the first execution, when the driver has reported them.

:param plan: plan to resolve processors for :type plan: StatementPlan :param dialect: dialect of the database :type dialect: Dialect :param coltypes: driver-reported column types (or None per column) :type coltypes: Sequence[Any]

Source code in ormar/databases/native/compiler.py Python
def resolve_result_processors(
    plan: StatementPlan, dialect: Dialect, coltypes: Sequence[Any]
) -> None:
    """
    Look up, once per plan, the result processor of each result column.

    A result processor is the function a SQLAlchemy type uses to turn the raw
    value a driver returns into the Python value of that type. Drivers return
    what the database stores, which is not always what the column type
    promises, e.g. on SQLite::

        DateTime  "2024-01-02 03:04:05" -> datetime(2024, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
        JSON      '{"a": 1}'            -> {"a": 1}
        Enum(C)   "red"                 -> C.red
        Boolean   1                     -> True
        Integer   needs none            -> None

    SQLAlchemy runs them on its own path; the native path must run the same
    ones, or rows would hold driver values. Some types pick their processor by
    the column type the driver reports (a PostgreSQL ``NUMERIC`` read into a
    ``Numeric(asdecimal=False)`` column needs a float conversion), so this runs
    on the first execution, when the driver has reported them.

    :param plan: plan to resolve processors for
    :type plan: StatementPlan
    :param dialect: dialect of the database
    :type dialect: Dialect
    :param coltypes: driver-reported column types (or None per column)
    :type coltypes: Sequence[Any]
    """
    plan.result_processors = [
        type_._cached_result_processor(dialect=dialect, coltype=coltype)
        for type_, coltype in zip(plan.result_types, coltypes)
    ]
    plan.processed_columns = tuple(
        (key, processor)
        for key, processor in zip(plan.result_keys, plan.result_processors)
        if processor is not None
    )

def row_class_for(result_columns: Sequence[Any]) -> type:
    """
    Build the ``NativeRow`` subclass of one plan, so its rows can be indexed by
    the selected column objects as well as by label.

    Column objects are matched by ``id()``, because ``==`` on a column builds a
    SQL expression instead of comparing. Each entry of SQLAlchemy's
    ``_result_columns`` lists the objects a result column was selected as::

        ResultColumnsEntry(keyname="name", objects=(Column("name", ...), ...))
        # -> object_keys == {id(users.c.name): "name", ...}

    :param result_columns: SQLAlchemy ``_result_columns`` of the statement
    :type result_columns: Sequence[Any]
    :return: ``NativeRow`` subclass for the plan
    :rtype: type
    """
    object_keys = {id(obj): column[0] for column in result_columns for obj in column[2]}
    return type("NativeRow", (NativeRow,), {"object_keys": object_keys})

def row_to_dict(plan: StatementPlan, values: Sequence[Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """
    Convert one driver row into a ``NativeRow`` keyed by result label, running
    each value through its result processor::

        (1, '{"a": 1}')  # -> {"id": 1, "data": {"a": 1}} on SQLite

    :param plan: plan of the executed statement, with resolved processors
    :type plan: StatementPlan
    :param values: row values in result column order
    :type values: Sequence[Any]
    :return: row keyed by result label
    :rtype: Dict[str, Any]
    """
    row = plan.row_class(zip(plan.result_keys, values))
    for key, processor in plan.processed_columns:
        row[key] = processor(row[key])
    return row  # type: ignore[no-any-return]

Text Only

{"my_col": 3}  # -> {"my col": 3}

def unescaped_view(
    compiled: SQLCompiler, params: MutableMapping[str, Any]
) -> MutableMapping[str, Any]:
    """
    Return the parameters keyed by the original bind names, as SQLAlchemy
    shows them to column defaults reading ``get_current_parameters()``.

    SQLAlchemy escapes bind names with characters a driver cannot take in a
    parameter name, and bound parameters use the escaped form::

        Column("my col", Integer)
        {"my_col": 3}  # -> {"my col": 3}

    :param compiled: compiled statement
    :type compiled: SQLCompiler
    :param params: parameters keyed by escaped bind names
    :type params: MutableMapping[str, Any]
    :return: parameters keyed by original bind names
    :rtype: MutableMapping[str, Any]
    """
    escaped = compiled.escaped_bind_names
    if not escaped:
        return params
    original = {value: key for key, value in escaped.items()}
    return {original.get(key, key): value for key, value in params.items()}

docs.title: raise_translated(error, *, backend, sa_connection, sql, args, ismulti=False) async
docs.text:
Re-raise a driver exception as the sqlalchemy.exc exception SQLAlchemy would raise for it, so user code catches the same errors on both paths::

Text Only
asyncpg.UniqueViolationError
# -> sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError: (...UniqueViolationError) duplicate key
#    [SQL: INSERT INTO users ...] [parameters: (...)]

When the dialect recognises the error as a lost connection, the connection is invalidated first, so it is closed instead of going back to the pool for the next query to fail on.

:param error: exception raised by the driver :type error: BaseException :param backend: native backend the statement ran on :type backend: NativeBackend :param sa_connection: connection the statement ran on :type sa_connection: AsyncConnection :param sql: executed SQL :type sql: str :param args: driver arguments of the statement (one list per row for batches) :type args: Sequence[Any] :param ismulti: whether the statement ran once per row of a batch :type ismulti: bool :raises sqlalchemy.exc.DBAPIError: always

Source code in ormar/databases/native/errors.py Python
async def raise_translated(
    error: BaseException,
    *,
    backend: NativeBackend,
    sa_connection: AsyncConnection,
    sql: str,
    args: Sequence[Any],
    ismulti: bool = False,
) -> NoReturn:
    """
    Re-raise a driver exception as the ``sqlalchemy.exc`` exception SQLAlchemy
    would raise for it, so user code catches the same errors on both paths::

        asyncpg.UniqueViolationError
        # -> sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError: (...UniqueViolationError) duplicate key
        #    [SQL: INSERT INTO users ...] [parameters: (...)]

    When the dialect recognises the error as a lost connection, the
    connection is invalidated first, so it is closed instead of going back to
    the pool for the next query to fail on.

    :param error: exception raised by the driver
    :type error: BaseException
    :param backend: native backend the statement ran on
    :type backend: NativeBackend
    :param sa_connection: connection the statement ran on
    :type sa_connection: AsyncConnection
    :param sql: executed SQL
    :type sql: str
    :param args: driver arguments of the statement (one list per row for batches)
    :type args: Sequence[Any]
    :param ismulti: whether the statement ran once per row of a batch
    :type ismulti: bool
    :raises sqlalchemy.exc.DBAPIError: always
    """
    raw = await sa_connection.get_raw_connection()
    dbapi_connection = raw.dbapi_connection
    orig = backend.adapter.translate_error(
        error=error, dbapi_connection=dbapi_connection
    )
    invalidated = backend.dialect.is_disconnect(
        e=orig,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
        connection=dbapi_connection,
        cursor=None,
    )
    if invalidated:
        await sa_connection.invalidate()  # pragma: no cover
    raise exc.DBAPIError.instance(
        statement=sql,
        params=list(args),
        orig=orig,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
        dbapi_base_err=backend.dialect.loaded_dbapi.Error,
        hide_parameters=sa_connection.sync_engine.hide_parameters,
        connection_invalidated=invalidated,
        dialect=backend.dialect,
        ismulti=ismulti,
    ) from orig

Only the drivers listed in ADAPTERS run natively; any other driver (e.g. aiomysql, aiopg) keeps running every statement through SQLAlchemy.

docs.title: DriverAdapter
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

Runs bound statements on one driver and returns results in the shape the SQLAlchemy path returns them (rows keyed by label, inserted pk, row count).

Every method takes raw, the pooled connection that SQLAlchemy's connection is using, so native statements share its transaction. It exposes two objects::

Text Only
# the driver's own connection, e.g. an asyncpg Connection
raw.driver_connection
# SQLAlchemy's wrapper around it, with the execution lock and the
# mapping of driver errors
raw.dbapi_connection

driver_errors lists the exceptions the driver raises, so the executor knows which ones to translate into SQLAlchemy exceptions.

Source code in ormar/databases/native/adapters/base.py Python
class DriverAdapter(abc.ABC):
    """
    Runs bound statements on one driver and returns results in the shape the
    SQLAlchemy path returns them (rows keyed by label, inserted pk, row count).

    Every method takes ``raw``, the pooled connection that SQLAlchemy's
    connection is using, so native statements share its transaction. It
    exposes two objects::

        # the driver's own connection, e.g. an asyncpg Connection
        raw.driver_connection
        # SQLAlchemy's wrapper around it, with the execution lock and the
        # mapping of driver errors
        raw.dbapi_connection

    ``driver_errors`` lists the exceptions the driver raises, so the executor
    knows which ones to translate into SQLAlchemy exceptions.
    """

    driver_errors: Tuple[Type[BaseException], ...]
    # True when the driver's executemany is all-or-nothing even outside a
    # transaction, so a single-batch bulk_create can skip opening one
    atomic_execute_many = False

    def __init__(self, dialect: Dialect) -> None:
        """
        :param dialect: dialect of the connected database
        :type dialect: Dialect
        """
        self.dialect = dialect

    @abc.abstractmethod
    async def fetch_all(self, raw: Any, bound: BoundStatement) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        """
        Run a statement and return all its rows keyed by result label::

            fetch_all(raw, bind(select(users.c.id, users.c.name)))
            # -> [{"id": 1, "name": "a"}, {"id": 2, "name": "b"}]

        :param raw: pooled raw connection
        :type raw: Any
        :param bound: statement to execute
        :type bound: BoundStatement
        :return: rows
        :rtype: List[Dict[str, Any]]
        """

    @abc.abstractmethod
    async def execute(self, raw: Any, bound: BoundStatement) -> Any:
        """
        Run an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE and return what SQLAlchemy's path would:
        the primary key of an inserted row, otherwise the number of rows changed::

            execute(raw, bind(users.insert().values(name="a")))  # -> 7 (new id)
            execute(raw, bind(users.delete()))  # -> 3 (rows deleted)

        :param raw: pooled raw connection
        :type raw: Any
        :param bound: statement to execute
        :type bound: BoundStatement
        :return: inserted primary key for INSERT, row count otherwise
        :rtype: Any
        """

    @abc.abstractmethod
    async def execute_many(self, raw: Any, batch: BoundBatch) -> None:
        """
        Run one statement once per row of arguments with the driver's
        ``executemany``, used by ``bulk_update``::

            stmt = users.update().where(users.c.id == bindparam("new_id"))
            stmt = stmt.values(name=bindparam("new_name"))
            rows = [{"new_id": 1, "new_name": "a"}, {"new_id": 2, "new_name": "b"}]
            execute_many(raw, bind_many(stmt, rows))

        :param raw: pooled raw connection
        :type raw: Any
        :param batch: statement and arguments per row
        :type batch: BoundBatch
        """

    @abc.abstractmethod
    def stream(
        self, raw: Any, bound: BoundStatement, batch_size: int
    ) -> AsyncGenerator[Dict[str, Any], None]:
        """
        Yield the rows of a statement one by one while fetching ``batch_size``
        rows per round trip, so ``QuerySet.iterate()`` never holds the whole
        result in memory.

        :param raw: pooled raw connection
        :type raw: Any
        :param bound: statement to execute
        :type bound: BoundStatement
        :param batch_size: rows fetched per round trip
        :type batch_size: int
        :return: rows keyed by result label
        :rtype: AsyncGenerator[Dict[str, Any], None]
        """

    async def start_transaction(self, sa_connection: AsyncConnection) -> None:
        """
        Make sure the transaction SQLAlchemy began is really open on the driver
        connection before native statements run on it.

        Some SQLAlchemy adapters only send ``BEGIN`` lazily with their own first
        statement; native statements bypass that, so without this they would run
        outside the transaction. No-op for drivers that start it on their own.

        :param sa_connection: connection the transaction was begun on
        :type sa_connection: AsyncConnection
        """

    def translate_error(
        self, error: BaseException, dbapi_connection: Any
    ) -> BaseException:
        """
        Return the exception SQLAlchemy's driver wrapper would raise for this
        driver error, which ``sqlalchemy.exc.DBAPIError.instance`` then wraps.

        SQLAlchemy maps driver exceptions to standard DBAPI classes before
        wrapping them, so users catch the same exception on both paths::

            asyncpg.UniqueViolationError -> IntegrityError
            # -> raised to the user as sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError

        Drivers that already raise DBAPI classes return the error unchanged.

        :param error: exception raised by the driver
        :type error: BaseException
        :param dbapi_connection: SQLAlchemy's adapted DBAPI connection
        :type dbapi_connection: Any
        :return: DBAPI-level exception
        :rtype: BaseException
        """
        return error

    def resolve_processors(self, bound: BoundStatement, coltypes: List[Any]) -> None:
        """
        Look up the plan's result processors on its first execution, once the
        driver has reported the result column types (see
        ``resolve_result_processors`` for what they are). Later executions reuse
        them.

        :param bound: executed statement
        :type bound: BoundStatement
        :param coltypes: driver-reported column types
        :type coltypes: List[Any]
        """
        if bound.plan.result_processors is None:
            resolve_result_processors(
                plan=bound.plan, dialect=self.dialect, coltypes=coltypes
            )

await driver.execute("SELECT users.id FROM users WHERE users.id = ?", [5])

class AiosqliteAdapter(DriverAdapter):
    """
    Runs bound statements on an aiosqlite connection, which takes ``?``-style
    SQL and a sequence of arguments::

        await driver.execute("SELECT users.id FROM users WHERE users.id = ?", [5])

    aiosqlite raises the standard ``sqlite3`` exceptions, which are DBAPI
    classes already, so they need no mapping. SQLite reports no column types,
    so result processors are looked up without them, as SQLAlchemy does.
    """

    def __init__(self, dialect: Dialect) -> None:
        """
        :param dialect: dialect of the connected database
        :type dialect: Dialect
        """
        super().__init__(dialect=dialect)
        self.driver_errors = (sqlite3.Error,)

    async def fetch_all(self, raw: Any, bound: BoundStatement) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        """
        Run a statement and return all rows keyed by result label.

        :param raw: pooled raw connection
        :type raw: Any
        :param bound: statement to execute
        :type bound: BoundStatement
        :return: rows
        :rtype: List[Dict[str, Any]]
        """
        async with execute_mutex(raw=raw):
            async with raw.driver_connection.execute(
                sql=bound.sql, parameters=bound.args
            ) as cursor:
                rows = await cursor.fetchall()
        self.resolve_processors(
            bound=bound, coltypes=[None] * len(bound.plan.result_keys)
        )
        return [row_to_dict(plan=bound.plan, values=row) for row in rows]

    async def execute(self, raw: Any, bound: BoundStatement) -> Any:
        """
        Run a write statement. The inserted primary key comes from ``RETURNING``
        when the statement has it (SQLite 3.35+), else from ``lastrowid``.

        :param raw: pooled raw connection
        :type raw: Any
        :param bound: statement to execute
        :type bound: BoundStatement
        :return: inserted primary key for INSERT, row count otherwise
        :rtype: Any
        """
        async with execute_mutex(raw=raw):
            async with raw.driver_connection.execute(
                sql=bound.sql, parameters=bound.args
            ) as cursor:
                returned = None
                if bound.plan.returning:
                    self.resolve_processors(
                        bound=bound, coltypes=[None] * len(bound.plan.result_keys)
                    )
                    returned = first_value(bound=bound, row=await cursor.fetchone())
                if bound.plan.is_insert:
                    return inserted_primary_key(
                        bound=bound, returned=returned, lastrowid=cursor.lastrowid
                    )
                return cursor.rowcount if cursor.rowcount is not None else 0

    async def execute_many(self, raw: Any, batch: BoundBatch) -> None:
        """
        Run a statement once per row with aiosqlite's ``executemany``.

        :param raw: pooled raw connection
        :type raw: Any
        :param batch: statement and arguments per row
        :type batch: BoundBatch
        """
        async with execute_mutex(raw=raw):
            await raw.driver_connection.executemany(
                sql=batch.sql, parameters=batch.args_list
            )

    async def stream(
        self, raw: Any, bound: BoundStatement, batch_size: int
    ) -> AsyncGenerator[Dict[str, Any], None]:
        """
        Stream rows of a statement, fetching ``batch_size`` rows at a time.
        No execution lock is taken: aiosqlite has none, as it runs every call
        in order on its own thread.

        :param raw: pooled raw connection
        :type raw: Any
        :param bound: statement to execute
        :type bound: BoundStatement
        :param batch_size: rows fetched per round trip
        :type batch_size: int
        :return: rows keyed by result label
        :rtype: AsyncGenerator[Dict[str, Any], None]
        """
        self.resolve_processors(
            bound=bound, coltypes=[None] * len(bound.plan.result_keys)
        )
        async with raw.driver_connection.execute(
            sql=bound.sql, parameters=bound.args
        ) as cursor:
            while rows := await cursor.fetchmany(size=batch_size):
                for row in rows:
                    yield row_to_dict(bound.plan, row)

Text Only
await cursor.execute("SELECT users.id FROM users WHERE users.id = %s", (5,))

Arguments are always passed as a tuple, even when empty. asyncmy only applies % formatting when arguments are given, and SQLAlchemy compiles a literal % as %%, so LIKE 'a%%' would otherwise reach MySQL with the %% intact.

class AsyncmyAdapter(DriverAdapter):
    """
    Runs bound statements on asyncmy cursors, which take ``%s``-style SQL and
    a tuple of arguments::

        await cursor.execute("SELECT users.id FROM users WHERE users.id = %s", (5,))

    Arguments are always passed as a tuple, even when empty. asyncmy only
    applies ``%`` formatting when arguments are given, and SQLAlchemy compiles
    a literal ``%`` as ``%%``, so ``LIKE 'a%%'`` would otherwise reach MySQL
    with the ``%%`` intact.
    """

    def __init__(self, dialect: Dialect) -> None:
        """
        :param dialect: dialect of the connected database
        :type dialect: Dialect
        """
        super().__init__(dialect=dialect)
        dbapi = dialect.dbapi
        # asyncmy raises AttributeError when its transport is gone mid-call;
        # SQLAlchemy's adapter turns it into a disconnect InternalError.
        self.driver_errors = (dbapi.Error, AttributeError)  # type: ignore[union-attr]
        self.unbuffered_cursor = dbapi.asyncmy.cursors.SSCursor  # type: ignore

    async def fetch_all(self, raw: Any, bound: BoundStatement) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        """
        Run a statement on a cursor and return all rows keyed by result label;
        the result column types come from ``cursor.description``.

        :param raw: pooled raw connection
        :type raw: Any
        :param bound: statement to execute
        :type bound: BoundStatement
        :return: rows
        :rtype: List[Dict[str, Any]]
        """
        async with execute_mutex(raw=raw), raw.driver_connection.cursor() as cursor:
            await cursor.execute(query=bound.sql, args=tuple(bound.args))
            self.resolve_processors(
                bound=bound, coltypes=[desc[1] for desc in cursor.description]
            )
            rows = await cursor.fetchall()
        return [row_to_dict(plan=bound.plan, values=row) for row in rows]

    async def execute(self, raw: Any, bound: BoundStatement) -> Any:
        """
        Run a write statement. MySQL has no ``RETURNING``, so a generated primary
        key comes from ``cursor.lastrowid`` and the row count from
        ``cursor.rowcount``.

        :param raw: pooled raw connection
        :type raw: Any
        :param bound: statement to execute
        :type bound: BoundStatement
        :return: inserted primary key for INSERT, row count otherwise
        :rtype: Any
        """
        async with execute_mutex(raw=raw), raw.driver_connection.cursor() as cursor:
            await cursor.execute(query=bound.sql, args=tuple(bound.args))
            if bound.plan.is_insert:
                return inserted_primary_key(
                    bound=bound, returned=None, lastrowid=cursor.lastrowid
                )
            return cursor.rowcount

    async def execute_many(self, raw: Any, batch: BoundBatch) -> None:
        """
        Run a statement once per row with the cursor's ``executemany``.

        :param raw: pooled raw connection
        :type raw: Any
        :param batch: statement and arguments per row
        :type batch: BoundBatch
        """
        async with execute_mutex(raw=raw), raw.driver_connection.cursor() as cursor:
            await cursor.executemany(
                query=batch.sql, args=[tuple(a) for a in batch.args_list]
            )

    async def stream(
        self, raw: Any, bound: BoundStatement, batch_size: int
    ) -> AsyncGenerator[Dict[str, Any], None]:
        """
        Stream rows through an unbuffered cursor (``SSCursor``), which reads
        rows from the network as they are fetched instead of loading the whole
        result first. The cursor is always closed at the end, because MySQL
        cannot run another statement on the connection while it is open.

        The execution lock is held per fetch only (see the asyncpg adapter).

        :param raw: pooled raw connection
        :type raw: Any
        :param bound: statement to execute
        :type bound: BoundStatement
        :param batch_size: rows fetched per round trip
        :type batch_size: int
        :return: rows keyed by result label
        :rtype: AsyncGenerator[Dict[str, Any], None]
        """
        cursor = raw.driver_connection.cursor(cursor=self.unbuffered_cursor)
        try:
            async with execute_mutex(raw=raw):
                await cursor.execute(query=bound.sql, args=tuple(bound.args))
                self.resolve_processors(
                    bound=bound, coltypes=[desc[1] for desc in cursor.description]
                )
            while True:
                async with execute_mutex(raw=raw):
                    rows = await cursor.fetchmany(size=batch_size)
                if not rows:
                    return
                for row in rows:
                    yield row_to_dict(plan=bound.plan, values=row)
        finally:
            async with execute_mutex(raw=raw):
                await cursor.close()

    def translate_error(
        self, error: BaseException, dbapi_connection: Any
    ) -> BaseException:
        """
        Map an asyncmy exception the way SQLAlchemy's asyncmy wrapper does.
        asyncmy raises ``AttributeError`` when its connection is gone in the
        middle of a call; the wrapper turns it into ``InternalError`` so the
        dialect recognises a disconnect and drops the connection.

        :param error: exception raised by asyncmy
        :type error: BaseException
        :param dbapi_connection: SQLAlchemy's adapted asyncmy connection
        :type dbapi_connection: Any
        :return: DBAPI-level exception
        :rtype: BaseException
        """
        try:
            dbapi_connection._handle_exception(error=error)
        except Exception as translated:
            return translated
        return error  # pragma: no cover
