class Query:
    """
    Builds the select of a queryset: joins of ``select_related``, selected
    columns, filters, ordering, limit and offset (with a pagination subquery
    when a limit meets ``select_related``).

    With a ``binder`` (see ``templates.SlotBinder``) every filter value, the
    limit and the offset are bound as named parameters, so the select can be
    cached as a statement template.
    """

    def __init__(  # noqa CFQ002
        self,
        model_cls: type["Model"],
        filter_clauses: list[FilterAction],
        exclude_clauses: list[FilterAction],
        select_related: list,
        limit_count: Optional[int],
        offset: Optional[int],
        excludable: "ExcludableItems",
        order_bys: Optional[list["OrderAction"]],
        limit_raw_sql: bool,
        binder: Optional["SlotBinder"] = None,
    ) -> None:
        self.query_offset = offset
        self.limit_count = limit_count
        self._select_related = select_related[:]
        self.filter_clauses = filter_clauses[:]
        self.exclude_clauses = exclude_clauses[:]
        self.excludable = excludable

        self.model_cls = model_cls
        self.table = self.model_cls.ormar_config.table

        self.used_aliases: list[str] = []

        self.select_from: Union[Join, Table, list[str]] = []
        self.columns: list[Column] = []
        self.order_columns = order_bys
        self.sorted_orders: dict[OrderAction, TextClause] = {}
        self._init_sorted_orders()

        self.limit_raw_sql = limit_raw_sql
        self.binder = binder

    def _init_sorted_orders(self) -> None:
        """
        Initialize empty order_by dict to be populated later during the query call
        """
        if self.order_columns:
            for clause in self.order_columns:
                self.sorted_orders[clause] = None  # type: ignore

    def apply_order_bys_for_primary_model(self) -> None:  # noqa: CCR001
        """
        Applies order_by queries on main model when it's used as a subquery.
        That way the subquery with limit and offset only on main model has proper
        sorting applied and correct models are fetched.
        """
        current_table_sorted = False
        if self.order_columns:
            for clause in self.order_columns:
                if clause.is_source_model_order:
                    current_table_sorted = True
                    self.sorted_orders[clause] = clause.get_text_clause()

        if not current_table_sorted:
            self._apply_default_model_sorting()

    def _apply_default_model_sorting(self) -> None:
        """
        Applies orders_by from model OrmarConfig (if provided), if it was not provided
        it was filled by metaclass, so it's always there and falls back to pk column
        """
        for clause in ormar.OrderAction.from_model_defaults(self.model_cls):
            self.sorted_orders[clause] = clause.get_text_clause()

    def _pagination_query_required(self) -> bool:
        """
        Checks if limit or offset are set, the flag limit_sql_raw is not set
        and query has select_related applied. Otherwise we can limit/offset normally
        at the end of whole query.

        :return: result of the check
        :rtype: bool
        """
        return bool(
            (self.limit_count or self.query_offset)
            and not self.limit_raw_sql
            and self._select_related
        )

    def build_select_expression(self) -> sqlalchemy.sql.Select:
        """
        Main entry point from outside (after proper initialization).

        Extracts columns list to fetch,
        construct all required joins for select related,
        then applies all conditional and sort clauses.

        Returns ready to run query with all joins and clauses.

        :return: ready to run query with all joins and clauses.
        :rtype: sqlalchemy.sql.selectable.Select
        """
        self_related_fields = self.model_cls.own_table_columns(
            model=self.model_cls, excludable=self.excludable, use_alias=True
        )
        self.columns = prefixed_columns("", self.table, self_related_fields)  # type: ignore
        self.apply_order_bys_for_primary_model()
        self.select_from = self.table

        related_models = group_related_list(self._select_related)

        for related in related_models:
            remainder = None
            if isinstance(related_models, dict) and related_models[related]:
                remainder = related_models[related]
            sql_join = SqlJoin(
                used_aliases=self.used_aliases,
                select_from=self.select_from,  # type: ignore
                columns=self.columns,
                excludable=self.excludable,
                order_columns=self.order_columns,
                sorted_orders=self.sorted_orders,
                main_model=self.model_cls,
                relation_name=related,
                relation_str=related,
                related_models=remainder,
            )

            (
                self.used_aliases,
                self.select_from,
                self.columns,
                self.sorted_orders,
            ) = sql_join.build_join()  # type: ignore

        if self._pagination_query_required():
            limit_qry, on_clause = self._build_pagination_condition()
            self.select_from = sqlalchemy.sql.join(
                cast("FromClauseRole", self.select_from), limit_qry, on_clause
            )

        expr = sqlalchemy.sql.select(*self.columns)
        expr = expr.select_from(cast("FromClauseRole", self.select_from))

        expr = self._apply_expression_modifiers(expr)

        # print("\n", expr.compile(compile_kwargs={"literal_binds": True}))
        self._reset_query_parameters()

        return expr

    def _build_pagination_condition(
        self,
    ) -> tuple[
        sqlalchemy.sql.expression.TextClause, sqlalchemy.sql.expression.TextClause
    ]:
        """
        In order to apply limit and offset on main table in join only
        (otherwise you can get only partially constructed main model
        if number of children exceeds the applied limit and select_related is used)

        Used also to change first and get() without argument behaviour.
        Needed only if limit or offset are set, the flag limit_sql_raw is not set
        and query has select_related applied. Otherwise we can limit/offset normally
        at the end of whole query.

        The condition is added to filters to filter out desired number of main model
        primary key values. Whole query is used to determine the values.
        """
        pk_alias = self.model_cls.get_column_alias(self.model_cls.ormar_config.pkname)
        pk_aliased_name = f"{self.table.name}.{pk_alias}"
        qry_text = sqlalchemy.text(f"{pk_aliased_name}")
        maxes = {}
        for order in list(self.sorted_orders.keys()):
            if order is not None and order.get_field_name_text() != pk_aliased_name:
                aliased_col = order.get_field_name_text()
                # maxes[aliased_col] = order.get_text_clause()
                maxes[aliased_col] = order.get_min_or_max()
            elif order.get_field_name_text() == pk_aliased_name:
                maxes[pk_aliased_name] = order.get_text_clause()

        limit_qry: Select[Any] = sqlalchemy.sql.select(qry_text)
        limit_qry = limit_qry.select_from(self.select_from)  # type: ignore
        limit_qry = FilterQuery(
            filter_clauses=self.filter_clauses, binder=self.binder
        ).apply(expr=limit_qry)
        limit_qry = FilterQuery(
            filter_clauses=self.exclude_clauses, exclude=True, binder=self.binder
        ).apply(expr=limit_qry)
        limit_qry = limit_qry.group_by(qry_text)
        for order_by in maxes.values():
            limit_qry = limit_qry.order_by(order_by)
        limit_qry = LimitQuery(limit_count=self.limit_count, binder=self.binder).apply(
            expr=limit_qry
        )
        limit_qry = OffsetQuery(
            query_offset=self.query_offset, binder=self.binder
        ).apply(expr=limit_qry)
        limit_qry = limit_qry.alias("limit_query")  # type: ignore
        on_clause = sqlalchemy.text(
            f"limit_query.{pk_alias}={self.table.name}.{pk_alias}"
        )
        return limit_qry, on_clause  # type: ignore

    def _apply_expression_modifiers(
        self, expr: sqlalchemy.sql.Select
    ) -> sqlalchemy.sql.Select:
        """
        Receives the select query (might be join) and applies:
        * Filter clauses
        * Exclude filter clauses
        * Limit clauses
        * Offset clauses
        * Order by clauses

        Returns complete ready to run query.

        :param expr: select expression before clauses
        :type expr: sqlalchemy.sql.selectable.Select
        :return: expression with all present clauses applied
        :rtype: sqlalchemy.sql.selectable.Select
        """
        expr = FilterQuery(
            filter_clauses=self.filter_clauses, binder=self.binder
        ).apply(expr=expr)
        expr = FilterQuery(
            filter_clauses=self.exclude_clauses, exclude=True, binder=self.binder
        ).apply(expr=expr)
        if not self._pagination_query_required():
            expr = LimitQuery(limit_count=self.limit_count, binder=self.binder).apply(
                expr=expr
            )
            expr = OffsetQuery(
                query_offset=self.query_offset, binder=self.binder
            ).apply(expr=expr)
        expr = OrderQuery(sorted_orders=self.sorted_orders).apply(expr)
        return expr

    def _reset_query_parameters(self) -> None:
        """
        Although it should be created each time before the call we reset the key params
        anyway.
        """
        self.select_from = []
        self.columns = []
        self.used_aliases = []

docs.text:
Statement templates: a statement built once per cache key and reused with new values on every later call.

Most of the cost of a simple read is building the statement: ormar walks the filters, joins, selected fields and ordering, and SQLAlchemy assembles the expression tree. Two calls that differ only in their values build the same tree, so QuerySet builds it once with named bind parameters ("slots") in place of the values and keeps it in a cache of the model::

Text Only
await Author.objects.filter(name="a").limit(5).all()
# built and cached: SELECT ... WHERE authors.name = :ormar_p0 LIMIT :ormar_limit
# bound this call:  {"ormar_p0": "a", "ormar_limit": 5}

await Author.objects.filter(name="b").limit(10).all()
# same cache key, statement reused: {"ormar_p0": "b", "ormar_limit": 10}

The cache key (see QuerySet.select_cache_key) holds everything that changes the SQL text and none of the bound values: filtered columns, operators, and/or/not nesting, select_related, selected fields, ordering and whether a limit or offset is present. Values SQLAlchemy writes into the SQL text instead of binding (None as IS NULL, booleans, isnull) are part of the key as well.

Writes are cached the same way. Model.save(), update(), delete(), load() and upsert() run one statement per model and set of written columns, binding the values as ormar_v{i} (in sorted column order) and the primary key as ormar_pk::

Text Only
await Author(name="a", score=1).save()
# INSERT INTO authors (name, score) VALUES (:ormar_v0, :ormar_v1)
# {"ormar_v0": "a", "ormar_v1": 1}

QuerySet.update() and delete() bind both filter and value slots, and bulk_create and bulk_update reuse one statement per set of columns for all their rows.

Running the same statement object every time also lets the native compiler reuse its plan for it instead of compiling the statement again.

The package is split by role:

  • cache - the per-model template cache
  • cache_keys - what makes two querysets share a statement
  • slots - named bind parameters and the values collected per call
  • reads - statements wrapped around a select, clean-up of templates
  • writes - single-row write templates and bulk statements

docs.text:
Turns per-call values of a read statement into named bind parameters while the statement is built. A filter action's value is named ormar_p{n} after its position among the canonical actions, limit and offset get fixed names::

Text Only
binder = SlotBinder(actions=[name_action, score_action])
binder.bind(action=score_action, value=5)  # -> :ormar_p1
binder.limit(value=10)  # -> :ormar_limit

Slots are looked up by action object, not by order of use, because one action can be emitted twice: with select_related and a limit, the filters go into the pagination subquery and the outer query, and both copies bind the same ormar_p{n}, so one value fills both.

Passed down through Query, FilterQuery, LimitQuery and OffsetQuery; without a binder they bind the plain values as before.

class SlotBinder:
    """
    Turns per-call values of a read statement into named bind parameters while
    the statement is built. A filter action's value is named ``ormar_p{n}``
    after its position among the canonical actions, limit and offset get fixed
    names::

        binder = SlotBinder(actions=[name_action, score_action])
        binder.bind(action=score_action, value=5)  # -> :ormar_p1
        binder.limit(value=10)  # -> :ormar_limit

    Slots are looked up by action object, not by order of use, because one
    action can be emitted twice: with ``select_related`` and a limit, the
    filters go into the pagination subquery and the outer query, and both
    copies bind the same ``ormar_p{n}``, so one value fills both.

    Passed down through ``Query``, ``FilterQuery``, ``LimitQuery`` and
    ``OffsetQuery``; without a binder they bind the plain values as before.
    """

    def __init__(self, actions: List["FilterAction"]) -> None:
        """
        :param actions: filter actions of the queryset in canonical order
        :type actions: List[FilterAction]
        """
        self.slots = {
            id(action): f"ormar_p{index}" for index, action in enumerate(actions)
        }

    def bind(self, action: "FilterAction", value: Any) -> BindParameter:
        """
        Return the named bind parameter for a filter action's value.

        The parameter is built the way SQLAlchemy builds the bind of
        ``column <op> value``: it is compared to the column's type, so the value
        gets the column's bind processing (dates, JSON, enums and so on), and
        an ``in`` filter is expanding, so it renders one placeholder per item of
        the list it is given on each call.

        :param action: filter action the value belongs to
        :type action: FilterAction
        :param value: value to bind
        :type value: Any
        :return: named bind parameter
        :rtype: BindParameter
        """
        operator = COMPARISON_OPERATORS[FILTER_OPERATORS[action.operator]]
        return BindParameter(
            key=self.slots[id(action)],
            value=value,
            expanding=action.operator == "in",
            _compared_to_operator=operator,
            _compared_to_type=action.column.type,
        )

    def limit(self, value: int) -> BindParameter:
        """
        Return the named bind parameter for a limit, typed as an integer like
        the one SQLAlchemy creates for ``select.limit(10)``.

        :param value: limit value
        :type value: int
        :return: named bind parameter
        :rtype: BindParameter
        """
        return sqlalchemy.bindparam(
            key=LIMIT_SLOT, value=value, type_=sqlalchemy.Integer()
        )

    def offset(self, value: int) -> BindParameter:
        """
        Return the named bind parameter for an offset, typed as an integer like
        the one SQLAlchemy creates for ``select.offset(10)``.

        :param value: offset value
        :type value: int
        :return: named bind parameter
        :rtype: BindParameter
        """
        return sqlalchemy.bindparam(
            key=OFFSET_SLOT, value=value, type_=sqlalchemy.Integer()
        )

docs.text:
Least-recently-used cache of one model's statements, keyed by cache key.

The size is bounded so an application that builds queries from many different filter combinations cannot grow memory without limit: once max_size keys are cached, adding one drops the key used longest ago.

Source code in ormar/queryset/templates/cache.py Python
class TemplateCache:
    """
    Least-recently-used cache of one model's statements, keyed by cache key.

    The size is bounded so an application that builds queries from many
    different filter combinations cannot grow memory without limit: once
    ``max_size`` keys are cached, adding one drops the key used longest ago.
    """

    def __init__(self, max_size: int = TEMPLATE_CACHE_SIZE) -> None:
        """
        :param max_size: number of cache keys kept
        :type max_size: int
        """
        self.max_size = max_size
        self.entries: "OrderedDict[Any, Any]" = OrderedDict()

    def get(self, key: Any) -> Any:
        """
        Return the statement cached for a key, or None, and mark it as the
        most recently used.

        Another thread using the same model may evict the entry between reading
        it and marking it, so that case is ignored: the statement is still
        valid for this call.

        :param key: cache key of the statement
        :type key: Any
        :return: cached statement or None
        :rtype: Any
        """
        statement = self.entries.get(key)
        if statement is not None:
            try:
                self.entries.move_to_end(key)
            except KeyError:  # pragma: no cover - evicted concurrently
                pass
        return statement

    def put(self, key: Any, statement: Any) -> None:
        """
        Cache the statement of a key. When the cache is full, the key used
        longest ago is dropped.

        :param key: cache key of the statement
        :type key: Any
        :param statement: statement to cache
        :type statement: Any
        """
        self.entries[key] = statement
        if len(self.entries) > self.max_size:
            self.entries.popitem(last=False)

    def clear(self) -> None:
        """Remove every cached statement."""
        self.entries.clear()

:param table: updated table :type table: sqlalchemy.Table :param pk_column: primary key column :type pk_column: sqlalchemy.Column :param columns: updated column names :type columns: Tuple[str, ...] :return: update statement :rtype: Executable

def build_bulk_update(
    table: sqlalchemy.Table, pk_column: sqlalchemy.Column, columns: Tuple[str, ...]
) -> Executable:
    """
    Build the per-row update used by ``bulk_update``: values and the primary
    key come from ``new_<column>`` parameters of each row, and the driver's
    ``executemany`` runs it once per row::

        UPDATE authors SET name=:new_name WHERE authors.id = :new_id
        # rows: [{"new_id": 1, "new_name": "a"}, {"new_id": 2, "new_name": "b"}]

    :param table: updated table
    :type table: sqlalchemy.Table
    :param pk_column: primary key column
    :type pk_column: sqlalchemy.Column
    :param columns: updated column names
    :type columns: Tuple[str, ...]
    :return: update statement
    :rtype: Executable
    """
    return (
        table.update()
        .where(pk_column == sqlalchemy.bindparam(key="new_" + pk_column.name))
        .values({name: sqlalchemy.bindparam(key="new_" + name) for name in columns})
    )

A write's cache key is small (the kind of statement and the written column names), so callers pass the key directly. The statement is only built on a miss, from builder(**builder_kwargs)::

:param model_cls: model the statement writes :type model_cls: Type[Any] :param key: cache key of the write :type key: Tuple[Any, ...] :param builder: builds the statement from builder_kwargs :type builder: Callable[..., Executable] :param builder_kwargs: keyword arguments of the builder :type builder_kwargs: Any :return: statement for the key :rtype: Executable

def cached_statement(
    model_cls: Type[Any],
    key: Tuple[Any, ...],
    builder: Callable[..., Executable],
    **builder_kwargs: Any,
) -> Executable:
    """
    Return the statement cached for a write cache key, building it on a miss.

    A write's cache key is small (the kind of statement and the written column
    names), so callers pass the key directly. The statement is only built on
    a miss, from ``builder(**builder_kwargs)``::

        cached_statement(
            model_cls=Author,
            key=("insert", ("name", "score")),
            builder=build_insert,
            table=Author.ormar_config.table,
            names=("name", "score"),
        )

    :param model_cls: model the statement writes
    :type model_cls: Type[Any]
    :param key: cache key of the write
    :type key: Tuple[Any, ...]
    :param builder: builds the statement from ``builder_kwargs``
    :type builder: Callable[..., Executable]
    :param builder_kwargs: keyword arguments of the builder
    :type builder_kwargs: Any
    :return: statement for the key
    :rtype: Executable
    """
    cache = template_cache_for(model_cls=model_cls)
    statement = cache.get(key)
    if statement is None:
        statement = builder(**builder_kwargs)
        cache.put(key=key, statement=statement)
    return statement

    first, then exclude clauses, each in build order::

    """
    Return the cache key of a list of filter actions and filter groups, keeping
    the and/or/not nesting, since ``or_(a, b)`` and ``and_(a, b)`` build
    different SQL from the same actions::

        filter(ormar.or_(name="a", score=1))
        # -> (("group", FilterType.OR, False, (), (<name key>, <score key>)),)

    :rtype: Tuple[Any, ...]

docs.text:
Wrap a read select into a row count, the statement run by QuerySet.count(). With distinct the rows are grouped by primary key first, so a model joined to several related rows is counted once::

Text Only
SELECT count(*) FROM (
    SELECT count(*) FROM (<select>) AS subquery_for_count GROUP BY <pk>
) AS subquery_for_group

:param select: read select of the queryset :type select: sqlalchemy.sql.Select :param distinct: count distinct primary keys only :type distinct: bool :param pk_column_name: primary key column alias of the model :type pk_column_name: str :return: count statement :rtype: Executable

Source code in ormar/queryset/templates/reads.py Python
def count_statement(
    select: sqlalchemy.sql.Select, distinct: bool, pk_column_name: str
) -> Executable:
    """
    Wrap a read select into a row count, the statement run by
    ``QuerySet.count()``. With ``distinct`` the rows are grouped by primary key
    first, so a model joined to several related rows is counted once::

        SELECT count(*) FROM (
            SELECT count(*) FROM (<select>) AS subquery_for_count GROUP BY <pk>
        ) AS subquery_for_group

    :param select: read select of the queryset
    :type select: sqlalchemy.sql.Select
    :param distinct: count distinct primary keys only
    :type distinct: bool
    :param pk_column_name: primary key column alias of the model
    :type pk_column_name: str
    :return: count statement
    :rtype: Executable
    """
    subquery = select.alias(name="subquery_for_count")
    expr = sqlalchemy.func.count().select().select_from(subquery)
    if distinct:
        grouped = expr.group_by(pk_column_name).alias(  # type: ignore[arg-type]
            name="subquery_for_group"
        )
        expr = sqlalchemy.func.count().select().select_from(grouped)
    return expr

filter(ormar.or_(ormar.and_(score=1, id=2), name="a"))
# -> score=1, id=2, name="a"

The order is the same for every queryset of one cache key, so an action's index here can name its slot.

:param clauses: filter actions and filter groups :type clauses: List[Union[FilterAction, FilterGroup]] :return: filter actions in build order :rtype: Iterator[FilterAction]

Source code in ormar/queryset/templates/slots.py Python
def iter_actions(
    clauses: List[Union["FilterAction", "FilterGroup"]],
) -> Iterator["FilterAction"]:
    """
    Yield the filter actions of a clause list in the order their SQL is built:
    a group's nested groups first, then its own actions (the order
    ``FilterGroup.get_text_clause`` emits them in)::

        filter(ormar.or_(ormar.and_(score=1, id=2), name="a"))
        # -> score=1, id=2, name="a"

    The order is the same for every queryset of one cache key, so an action's
    index here can name its slot.

    :param clauses: filter actions and filter groups
    :type clauses: List[Union[FilterAction, FilterGroup]]
    :return: filter actions in build order
    :rtype: Iterator[FilterAction]
    """
    for clause in clauses:
        if hasattr(clause, "_nested_groups"):
            yield from iter_actions(clauses=clause._nested_groups)  # type: ignore
            yield from clause.actions  # type: ignore
        else:
            yield clause  # type: ignore

def release_values(statement: Executable) -> None:
    """
    Drop the values of a template's named slots, so a cached statement does
    not keep the first call's values (possibly large lists or documents) alive
    for as long as it stays cached. Every call binds its own values anyway.

    SQLAlchemy may have cloned the bind parameters while wrapping the select
    (for example into a subquery), so the whole statement is walked instead of
    clearing only the parameters ``SlotBinder`` created.

    :param statement: built template statement
    :type statement: Executable
    """
    for element in visitors.iterate(statement):  # type: ignore[arg-type]
        if isinstance(element, BindParameter) and str(element.key).startswith("ormar_"):
            element.value = None

:param actions: filter actions in canonical order :type actions: List[FilterAction] :param limit: effective limit (applied when not None) :type limit: Optional[int] :param offset: effective offset (applied when truthy) :type offset: Optional[int] :return: values per slot name :rtype: Dict[str, Any]

def template_params(
    actions: List["FilterAction"], limit: Optional[int], offset: Optional[int]
) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """
    Collect the values a template binds for one call, keyed like the slots
    ``SlotBinder`` names::

        Author.objects.filter(name="a", score__gt=5).limit(10)
        # -> {"ormar_p0": "a", "ormar_p1": 5, "ormar_limit": 10}

    Actions whose value is written into the SQL text (see
    ``FilterAction.binds_slot``) get no entry, but still use up their index,
    so the names of the other slots do not depend on those values. The offset
    is only bound when non-zero, matching ``OffsetQuery``, which leaves out
    ``OFFSET 0``.

    :param actions: filter actions in canonical order
    :type actions: List[FilterAction]
    :param limit: effective limit (applied when not None)
    :type limit: Optional[int]
    :param offset: effective offset (applied when truthy)
    :type offset: Optional[int]
    :return: values per slot name
    :rtype: Dict[str, Any]
    """
    params = {}
    for index, action in enumerate(actions):
        if action.binds_slot():
            params[f"ormar_p{index}"] = action.bound_value()
    if limit is not None:
        params[LIMIT_SLOT] = limit
    if offset:
        params[OFFSET_SLOT] = offset
    return params

Return the part of a filter value that changes the SQL text::

Text Only
filter(name__isnull=True)  # -> ("isnull", True)   IS NULL
filter(name=None)  # -> ("literal", None)  IS NULL
filter(active=True)  # -> ("literal", True)  literal true
filter(id__in=[1, 2])  # -> "in"               IN (expanding)
filter(name="a")  # -> ("value", str)     = :ormar_p0

Values written into the SQL text are part of the key as they are. For a bound value only its type is kept, so values of different types never share a statement.

:param action: filter action :type action: FilterAction :return: hashable value kind :rtype: Any

Source code in ormar/queryset/templates/cache_keys.py Python
def value_cache_key(action: "FilterAction") -> Any:
    """
    Return the part of a filter value that changes the SQL text::

        filter(name__isnull=True)  # -> ("isnull", True)   IS NULL
        filter(name=None)  # -> ("literal", None)  IS NULL
        filter(active=True)  # -> ("literal", True)  literal true
        filter(id__in=[1, 2])  # -> "in"               IN (expanding)
        filter(name="a")  # -> ("value", str)     = :ormar_p0

    Values written into the SQL text are part of the key as they are. For a
    bound value only its type is kept, so values of different types never
    share a statement.

    :param action: filter action
    :type action: FilterAction
    :return: hashable value kind
    :rtype: Any
    """
    value = action.bound_value()
    if action.operator == "isnull":
        return ("isnull", bool(value))
    if action.operator == "in":
        return "in"
    if not action.binds_slot():
        return ("literal", value)
    return ("value", type(value))

docs.text:
Least-recently-used cache of one model's statements, keyed by cache key.

The size is bounded so an application that builds queries from many different filter combinations cannot grow memory without limit: once max_size keys are cached, adding one drops the key used longest ago.

Source code in ormar/queryset/templates/cache.py Python
class TemplateCache:
    """
    Least-recently-used cache of one model's statements, keyed by cache key.

    The size is bounded so an application that builds queries from many
    different filter combinations cannot grow memory without limit: once
    ``max_size`` keys are cached, adding one drops the key used longest ago.
    """

    def __init__(self, max_size: int = TEMPLATE_CACHE_SIZE) -> None:
        """
        :param max_size: number of cache keys kept
        :type max_size: int
        """
        self.max_size = max_size
        self.entries: "OrderedDict[Any, Any]" = OrderedDict()

    def get(self, key: Any) -> Any:
        """
        Return the statement cached for a key, or None, and mark it as the
        most recently used.

        Another thread using the same model may evict the entry between reading
        it and marking it, so that case is ignored: the statement is still
        valid for this call.

        :param key: cache key of the statement
        :type key: Any
        :return: cached statement or None
        :rtype: Any
        """
        statement = self.entries.get(key)
        if statement is not None:
            try:
                self.entries.move_to_end(key)
            except KeyError:  # pragma: no cover - evicted concurrently
                pass
        return statement

    def put(self, key: Any, statement: Any) -> None:
        """
        Cache the statement of a key. When the cache is full, the key used
        longest ago is dropped.

        :param key: cache key of the statement
        :type key: Any
        :param statement: statement to cache
        :type statement: Any
        """
        self.entries[key] = statement
        if len(self.entries) > self.max_size:
            self.entries.popitem(last=False)

    def clear(self) -> None:
        """Remove every cached statement."""
        self.entries.clear()

def cached_statement(
    model_cls: Type[Any],
    key: Tuple[Any, ...],
    builder: Callable[..., Executable],
    **builder_kwargs: Any,
) -> Executable:
    """
    Return the statement cached for a write cache key, building it on a miss.

    A write's cache key is small (the kind of statement and the written column
    names), so callers pass the key directly. The statement is only built on
    a miss, from ``builder(**builder_kwargs)``::

        cached_statement(
            model_cls=Author,
            key=("insert", ("name", "score")),
            builder=build_insert,
            table=Author.ormar_config.table,
            names=("name", "score"),
        )

    :param model_cls: model the statement writes
    :type model_cls: Type[Any]
    :param key: cache key of the write
    :type key: Tuple[Any, ...]
    :param builder: builds the statement from ``builder_kwargs``
    :type builder: Callable[..., Executable]
    :param builder_kwargs: keyword arguments of the builder
    :type builder_kwargs: Any
    :return: statement for the key
    :rtype: Executable
    """
    cache = template_cache_for(model_cls=model_cls)
    statement = cache.get(key)
    if statement is None:
        statement = builder(**builder_kwargs)
        cache.put(key=key, statement=statement)
    return statement

Cache keys of statement templates: hashable values holding everything about a queryset that changes its SQL text and none of its bound values.

Two querysets with equal keys must build the same SQL, or one would run the other's statement. QuerySet.select_cache_key combines these keys for reads, QuerySet.build_write_template for filtered updates and deletes::

Text Only
Author.objects.filter(name="a")  # same key as filter(name="b")
Author.objects.filter(name=None)  # different key: renders IS NULL

:param action: filter action :type action: FilterAction :return: hashable cache key of the action :rtype: Tuple[Any, ...]

def action_cache_key(action: "FilterAction") -> Tuple[Any, ...]:
    """
    Return everything about a filter action that changes the SQL text: the
    field path, the table alias of the joined relation, the operator, the
    kind of value (see ``value_cache_key``) and whether LIKE needs an ``ESCAPE``
    clause for ``%`` or ``_`` in the value.

    :param action: filter action
    :type action: FilterAction
    :return: hashable cache key of the action

docs.text:
Return the cache key of a list of filter actions and filter groups, keeping the and/or/not nesting, since or_(a, b) and and_(a, b) build different SQL from the same actions::

Text Only
filter(ormar.or_(name="a", score=1))
# -> (("group", FilterType.OR, False, (), (<name key>, <score key>)),)

:param clauses: filter actions and filter groups :type clauses: Iterable[Any] :return: hashable cache key of the clauses :rtype: Tuple[Any, ...]

def clauses_cache_key(clauses: Iterable[Any]) -> Tuple[Any, ...]:
    """
    Return the cache key of a list of filter actions and filter groups, keeping
    the and/or/not nesting, since ``or_(a, b)`` and ``and_(a, b)`` build
    different SQL from the same actions::

        filter(ormar.or_(name="a", score=1))
        # -> (("group", FilterType.OR, False, (), (<name key>, <score key>)),)

    :param clauses: filter actions and filter groups
    :type clauses: Iterable[Any]
    :return: hashable cache key of the clauses
    :rtype: Tuple[Any, ...]
    """
    return tuple(
        (
            "group",
            clause.filter_type,
            clause.exclude,
            clauses_cache_key(clauses=clause._nested_groups),
            tuple(action_cache_key(action=action) for action in clause.actions),
        )
        if hasattr(clause, "_nested_groups")
        else action_cache_key(action=clause)
        for clause in clauses
    )

    """
    Return the fields included and excluded per model and relation, which
    decide the selected columns (``fields()``, ``exclude_fields()``,
    ``values()``). Field sets are sorted so the same selection always gives
    the same key.

    :param excludable: queryset's fields to include and exclude

            tuple(sorted(item.include, key=repr)),
            tuple(sorted(item.exclude, key=repr)),
            tuple(sorted(item.flatten, key=repr)),

docs.title: value_cache_key(action)
docs.text:
Return the part of a filter value that changes the SQL text::

Text Only
filter(name__isnull=True)  # -> ("isnull", True)   IS NULL
filter(name=None)  # -> ("literal", None)  IS NULL
filter(active=True)  # -> ("literal", True)  literal true
filter(id__in=[1, 2])  # -> "in"               IN (expanding)
filter(name="a")  # -> ("value", str)     = :ormar_p0

Values written into the SQL text are part of the key as they are. For a bound value only its type is kept, so values of different types never share a statement.

:param action: filter action :type action: FilterAction :return: hashable value kind :rtype: Any

Source code in ormar/queryset/templates/cache_keys.py Python
def value_cache_key(action: "FilterAction") -> Any:
    """
    Return the part of a filter value that changes the SQL text::

        filter(name__isnull=True)  # -> ("isnull", True)   IS NULL
        filter(name=None)  # -> ("literal", None)  IS NULL
        filter(active=True)  # -> ("literal", True)  literal true
        filter(id__in=[1, 2])  # -> "in"               IN (expanding)
        filter(name="a")  # -> ("value", str)     = :ormar_p0

    Values written into the SQL text are part of the key as they are. For a
    bound value only its type is kept, so values of different types never
    share a statement.

    :param action: filter action
    :type action: FilterAction
    :return: hashable value kind
    :rtype: Any
    """
    value = action.bound_value()
    if action.operator == "isnull":
        return ("isnull", bool(value))
    if action.operator == "in":
        return "in"
    if not action.binds_slot():
        return ("literal", value)
    return ("value", type(value))

def aggregate_statement(
    select: sqlalchemy.sql.Select, func_name: str, select_columns: List[Any]
) -> Executable:
    """
    Wrap a read select into aggregate function columns, the statement run by
    ``QuerySet.max()``, ``min()``, ``sum()`` and ``avg()``::

        SELECT max(subquery_for_max.score) AS score
        FROM (<select>) AS subquery_for_max

    :param select: read select of the queryset
    :type select: sqlalchemy.sql.Select
    :param func_name: aggregate function name
    :type func_name: str

    :return: aggregate statement

docs.title: count_statement(select, distinct, pk_column_name)
docs.text:
Wrap a read select into a row count, the statement run by QuerySet.count(). With distinct the rows are grouped by primary key first, so a model joined to several related rows is counted once::

Text Only
SELECT count(*) FROM (
    SELECT count(*) FROM (<select>) AS subquery_for_count GROUP BY <pk>
) AS subquery_for_group

:param select: read select of the queryset :type select: sqlalchemy.sql.Select :param distinct: count distinct primary keys only :type distinct: bool :param pk_column_name: primary key column alias of the model :type pk_column_name: str :return: count statement :rtype: Executable

Source code in ormar/queryset/templates/reads.py Python
def count_statement(
    select: sqlalchemy.sql.Select, distinct: bool, pk_column_name: str
) -> Executable:
    """
    Wrap a read select into a row count, the statement run by
    ``QuerySet.count()``. With ``distinct`` the rows are grouped by primary key
    first, so a model joined to several related rows is counted once::

        SELECT count(*) FROM (
            SELECT count(*) FROM (<select>) AS subquery_for_count GROUP BY <pk>
        ) AS subquery_for_group

    :param select: read select of the queryset
    :type select: sqlalchemy.sql.Select
    :param distinct: count distinct primary keys only
    :type distinct: bool
    :param pk_column_name: primary key column alias of the model
    :type pk_column_name: str
    :return: count statement
    :rtype: Executable
    """
    subquery = select.alias(name="subquery_for_count")
    expr = sqlalchemy.func.count().select().select_from(subquery)
    if distinct:
        grouped = expr.group_by(pk_column_name).alias(  # type: ignore[arg-type]
            name="subquery_for_group"
        )
        expr = sqlalchemy.func.count().select().select_from(grouped)
    return expr

docs.title: release_values(statement)
docs.text:
Drop the values of a template's named slots, so a cached statement does not keep the first call's values (possibly large lists or documents) alive for as long as it stays cached. Every call binds its own values anyway.

SQLAlchemy may have cloned the bind parameters while wrapping the select (for example into a subquery), so the whole statement is walked instead of clearing only the parameters SlotBinder created.

:param statement: built template statement :type statement: Executable

Source code in ormar/queryset/templates/reads.py Python
def release_values(statement: Executable) -> None:
    """
    Drop the values of a template's named slots, so a cached statement does
    not keep the first call's values (possibly large lists or documents) alive
    for as long as it stays cached. Every call binds its own values anyway.

    SQLAlchemy may have cloned the bind parameters while wrapping the select
    (for example into a subquery), so the whole statement is walked instead of
    clearing only the parameters ``SlotBinder`` created.

    :param statement: built template statement
    :type statement: Executable
    """
    for element in visitors.iterate(statement):  # type: ignore[arg-type]
        if isinstance(element, BindParameter) and str(element.key).startswith("ormar_"):
            element.value = None

docs.title: slots
docs.text:
Slots: named bind parameters that take the per-call values of a statement template.

While a template is built, SlotBinder puts slots in place of the values (filters as ormar_p{n}, limit and offset as ormar_limit and ormar_offset). Writes bind values as ormar_v{i} and the primary key as ormar_pk. On every call the values are collected under the same names::

Text Only
SELECT ... WHERE authors.name = :ormar_p0 LIMIT :ormar_limit
# {"ormar_p0": "a", "ormar_limit": 5}

docs.title: SlotBinder
docs.text:
Turns per-call values of a read statement into named bind parameters while the statement is built. A filter action's value is named ormar_p{n} after its position among the canonical actions, limit and offset get fixed names::

Text Only
binder = SlotBinder(actions=[name_action, score_action])
binder.bind(action=score_action, value=5)  # -> :ormar_p1
binder.limit(value=10)  # -> :ormar_limit

Slots are looked up by action object, not by order of use, because one action can be emitted twice: with select_related and a limit, the filters go into the pagination subquery and the outer query, and both copies bind the same ormar_p{n}, so one value fills both.

Passed down through Query, FilterQuery, LimitQuery and OffsetQuery; without a binder they bind the plain values as before.

Source code in ormar/queryset/templates/slots.py Python
class SlotBinder:
    """
    Turns per-call values of a read statement into named bind parameters while
    the statement is built. A filter action's value is named ``ormar_p{n}``
    after its position among the canonical actions, limit and offset get fixed
    names::

        binder = SlotBinder(actions=[name_action, score_action])
        binder.bind(action=score_action, value=5)  # -> :ormar_p1
        binder.limit(value=10)  # -> :ormar_limit

    Slots are looked up by action object, not by order of use, because one
    action can be emitted twice: with ``select_related`` and a limit, the
    filters go into the pagination subquery and the outer query, and both
    copies bind the same ``ormar_p{n}``, so one value fills both.

    Passed down through ``Query``, ``FilterQuery``, ``LimitQuery`` and
    ``OffsetQuery``; without a binder they bind the plain values as before.
    """

    def __init__(self, actions: List["FilterAction"]) -> None:
        """
        :param actions: filter actions of the queryset in canonical order
        :type actions: List[FilterAction]
        """
        self.slots = {
            id(action): f"ormar_p{index}" for index, action in enumerate(actions)
        }

    def bind(self, action: "FilterAction", value: Any) -> BindParameter:
        """
        Return the named bind parameter for a filter action's value.

        The parameter is built the way SQLAlchemy builds the bind of
        ``column <op> value``: it is compared to the column's type, so the value
        gets the column's bind processing (dates, JSON, enums and so on), and
        an ``in`` filter is expanding, so it renders one placeholder per item of
        the list it is given on each call.

        :param action: filter action the value belongs to
        :type action: FilterAction
        :param value: value to bind
        :type value: Any
        :return: named bind parameter
        :rtype: BindParameter
        """
        operator = COMPARISON_OPERATORS[FILTER_OPERATORS[action.operator]]
        return BindParameter(
            key=self.slots[id(action)],
            value=value,
            expanding=action.operator == "in",
            _compared_to_operator=operator,
            _compared_to_type=action.column.type,
        )

    def limit(self, value: int) -> BindParameter:
        """
        Return the named bind parameter for a limit, typed as an integer like
        the one SQLAlchemy creates for ``select.limit(10)``.

        :param value: limit value
        :type value: int
        :return: named bind parameter
        :rtype: BindParameter
        """
        return sqlalchemy.bindparam(
            key=LIMIT_SLOT, value=value, type_=sqlalchemy.Integer()
        )

    def offset(self, value: int) -> BindParameter:
        """
        Return the named bind parameter for an offset, typed as an integer like
        the one SQLAlchemy creates for ``select.offset(10)``.

        :param value: offset value
        :type value: int
        :return: named bind parameter
        :rtype: BindParameter
        """
        return sqlalchemy.bindparam(
            key=OFFSET_SLOT, value=value, type_=sqlalchemy.Integer()
        )

def canonical_actions(
    filter_clauses: List[Any], exclude_clauses: List[Any]
) -> List["FilterAction"]:
    """
    Return every filter action of a queryset in canonical order: filter clauses
    first, then exclude clauses, each in build order::

        Author.objects.exclude(score=0).filter(name="a")
        # -> name="a" (ormar_p0), score=0 (ormar_p1)

    ``SlotBinder`` (naming the slots while building) and ``template_params``
    (collecting values on every call) both use this list, so a value always
    ends up in the slot built for it.

    :param filter_clauses: queryset filter clauses
    :type filter_clauses: List[Any]
    :param exclude_clauses: queryset exclude clauses
    :type exclude_clauses: List[Any]
    :return: filter actions in canonical order
    :rtype: List[FilterAction]
    """
    return [
        *iter_actions(clauses=filter_clauses),
        *iter_actions(clauses=exclude_clauses),

docs.title: iter_actions(clauses)
docs.text:
Yield the filter actions of a clause list in the order their SQL is built: a group's nested groups first, then its own actions (the order FilterGroup.get_text_clause emits them in)::

Text Only
filter(ormar.or_(ormar.and_(score=1, id=2), name="a"))
# -> score=1, id=2, name="a"

The order is the same for every queryset of one cache key, so an action's index here can name its slot.

:param clauses: filter actions and filter groups :type clauses: List[Union[FilterAction, FilterGroup]] :return: filter actions in build order :rtype: Iterator[FilterAction]

Source code in ormar/queryset/templates/slots.py Python
def iter_actions(
    clauses: List[Union["FilterAction", "FilterGroup"]],
) -> Iterator["FilterAction"]:
    """
    Yield the filter actions of a clause list in the order their SQL is built:
    a group's nested groups first, then its own actions (the order
    ``FilterGroup.get_text_clause`` emits them in)::

        filter(ormar.or_(ormar.and_(score=1, id=2), name="a"))
        # -> score=1, id=2, name="a"

    The order is the same for every queryset of one cache key, so an action's
    index here can name its slot.

    :param clauses: filter actions and filter groups
    :type clauses: List[Union[FilterAction, FilterGroup]]
    :return: filter actions in build order
    :rtype: Iterator[FilterAction]
    """
    for clause in clauses:
        if hasattr(clause, "_nested_groups"):
            yield from iter_actions(clauses=clause._nested_groups)  # type: ignore
            yield from clause.actions  # type: ignore
        else:
            yield clause  # type: ignore

docs.title: template_params(actions, limit, offset)
docs.text:
Collect the values a template binds for one call, keyed like the slots SlotBinder names::

Text Only
Author.objects.filter(name="a", score__gt=5).limit(10)
# -> {"ormar_p0": "a", "ormar_p1": 5, "ormar_limit": 10}

Actions whose value is written into the SQL text (see FilterAction.binds_slot) get no entry, but still use up their index, so the names of the other slots do not depend on those values. The offset is only bound when non-zero, matching OffsetQuery, which leaves out OFFSET 0.

:param actions: filter actions in canonical order :type actions: List[FilterAction] :param limit: effective limit (applied when not None) :type limit: Optional[int] :param offset: effective offset (applied when truthy) :type offset: Optional[int] :return: values per slot name :rtype: Dict[str, Any]

def template_params(
    actions: List["FilterAction"], limit: Optional[int], offset: Optional[int]
) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """
    Collect the values a template binds for one call, keyed like the slots
    ``SlotBinder`` names::

        Author.objects.filter(name="a", score__gt=5).limit(10)
        # -> {"ormar_p0": "a", "ormar_p1": 5, "ormar_limit": 10}

    Actions whose value is written into the SQL text (see
    ``FilterAction.binds_slot``) get no entry, but still use up their index,
    so the names of the other slots do not depend on those values. The offset
    is only bound when non-zero, matching ``OffsetQuery``, which leaves out
    ``OFFSET 0``.

    :param actions: filter actions in canonical order
    :type actions: List[FilterAction]
    :param limit: effective limit (applied when not None)
    :type limit: Optional[int]
    :param offset: effective offset (applied when truthy)
    :type offset: Optional[int]
    :return: values per slot name
    :rtype: Dict[str, Any]
    """
    params = {}
    for index, action in enumerate(actions):
        if action.binds_slot():
            params[f"ormar_p{index}"] = action.bound_value()
    if limit is not None:
        params[LIMIT_SLOT] = limit
    if offset:
        params[OFFSET_SLOT] = offset
    return params

:param table: updated table :type table: sqlalchemy.Table :param pk_column: primary key column :type pk_column: sqlalchemy.Column :param columns: updated column names :type columns: Tuple[str, ...] :return: update statement :rtype: Executable

def build_bulk_update(
    table: sqlalchemy.Table, pk_column: sqlalchemy.Column, columns: Tuple[str, ...]
) -> Executable:
    """
    Build the per-row update used by ``bulk_update``: values and the primary
    key come from ``new_<column>`` parameters of each row, and the driver's
    ``executemany`` runs it once per row::

        UPDATE authors SET name=:new_name WHERE authors.id = :new_id
        # rows: [{"new_id": 1, "new_name": "a"}, {"new_id": 2, "new_name": "b"}]

    :param table: updated table
    :type table: sqlalchemy.Table
    :param pk_column: primary key column
    :type pk_column: sqlalchemy.Column
    :param columns: updated column names
    :type columns: Tuple[str, ...]
    :return: update statement
    :rtype: Executable
    """
    return (
        table.update()
        .where(pk_column == sqlalchemy.bindparam(key="new_" + pk_column.name))
        .values({name: sqlalchemy.bindparam(key="new_" + name) for name in columns})
    )

    column = PK_COLUMNS.get(model_cls)

docs.text: Package handles relations on models, returning related models on calls and exposing QuerySetProxy for m2m and reverse relations.

docs.title: Relation
docs.text:
Bases: Generic[T]

Keeps related Models and handles adding/removing of the children.

Source code in ormar/relations/relation.py Python
class Relation(Generic[T]):
    """
    Keeps related Models and handles adding/removing of the children.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        manager: "RelationsManager",
        type_: RelationType,
        field_name: str,
        to: type["T"],
        through: Optional[type["Model"]] = None,
    ) -> None:
        """
        Initialize the Relation and keep the related models either as instances of
        passed Model, or as a RelationProxy which is basically a list of models with
        some special behavior, as it exposes QuerySetProxy and allows querying the
        related models already pre filtered by parent model.

        :param manager: reference to relation manager
        :type manager: RelationsManager
        :param type_: type of the relation
        :type type_: RelationType
        :param field_name: name of the relation field
        :type field_name: str
        :param to: model to which relation leads to
        :type to: type[Model]
        :param through: model through which relation goes for m2m relations
        :type through: type[Model]
        """
        self.manager = manager
        self._owner: "Model" = manager.owner
        self._type: RelationType = type_
        self._to_remove: set = set()
        self.to: type["T"] = to
        self._through = through
        self.field_name: str = field_name
        # ``RelationProxy`` is built lazily on the first reverse/m2m use
        # (``add`` / ``get`` / ``_clean_related``) to avoid the per-model
        # allocation when the relation is never read.
        self.related_models: Optional[Union[RelationProxy, "Model"]] = None

    def _ensure_proxy(self) -> RelationProxy:
        """
        Materialize and cache the ``RelationProxy`` for reverse/m2m relations
        on first use. Safe to call multiple times — subsequent calls return
        the cached proxy.

        :return: the relation's ``RelationProxy``
        :rtype: RelationProxy
        """
        proxy = self.related_models
        if not isinstance(proxy, RelationProxy):
            proxy = RelationProxy(
                relation=self,
                type_=self._type,
                to=self.to,
                field_name=self.field_name,
            )
            self.related_models = proxy
        return proxy

    def clear(self) -> None:
        if self._type in (RelationType.PRIMARY, RelationType.THROUGH):
            self.related_models = None
            self._owner.__dict__[self.field_name] = None
        elif self.related_models is not None:
            related_models = cast("RelationProxy", self.related_models)
            related_models._clear()
            self._owner.__dict__[self.field_name] = None

    @property
    def through(self) -> type["Model"]:
        if not self._through:  # pragma: no cover
            raise RelationshipInstanceError("Relation does not have through model!")
        return self._through

    def _clean_related(self) -> None:
        """
        Removes dead weakrefs from RelationProxy.
        """
        cleaned_data = [
            x
            for i, x in enumerate(self.related_models)  # type: ignore
            if i not in self._to_remove
        ]
        proxy = RelationProxy(
            relation=self,
            type_=self._type,
            to=self.to,
            field_name=self.field_name,
            data_=cleaned_data,
        )
        self.related_models = proxy
        self._owner.__dict__[self.field_name] = proxy
        self._to_remove = set()

    def _find_existing(
        self, child: Union["NewBaseModel", type["NewBaseModel"]]
    ) -> Optional[int]:
        """
        Find child model in RelationProxy if exists.

        :param child: child model to find
        :type child: Model
        :return: index of child in RelationProxy
        :rtype: Optional[ind]
        """
        if not isinstance(self.related_models, RelationProxy):  # pragma nocover
            raise ValueError("Cannot find existing models in parent relation type")

        if child not in self.related_models:
            return None
        else:
            # We need to clear the weakrefs that don't point to anything anymore
            # There's an assumption here that if some of the related models
            # went out of scope, then they all did, so we can just check the first one
            try:
                self.related_models[0].__repr__.__self__
                return self.related_models.index(child)
            except ReferenceError:
                missing = self.related_models._get_list_of_missing_weakrefs()
                self._to_remove.update(missing)
            return self.related_models.index(child)

    def add(self, child: "Model") -> None:
        """
        Adds child Model to relation, either sets child as related model or adds
        it to the list in RelationProxy depending on relation type.

        For reverse / many-to-many relations the ``RelationProxy`` itself is
        stored under ``_owner.__dict__[relation_name]``, so a single O(1)
        membership check on the proxy's hash cache covers both the relation
        bookkeeping and the pydantic-visible ``__dict__`` slot — no parallel
        list, no second linear scan.

        :param child: model to add to relation
        :type child: Model
        """
        relation_name = self.field_name
        if self._type in (RelationType.PRIMARY, RelationType.THROUGH):
            self.related_models = child
            self._owner.__dict__[relation_name] = child
            return
        proxy = self._ensure_proxy()
        # ``_find_existing`` is the membership check *plus* a dead-weakref
        # probe — when a hash collision lands on a stale entry we need that
        # probe to populate ``_to_remove`` so the next ``get()`` triggers
        # ``_clean_related``.
        if self._find_existing(child) is None:
            proxy.append(child)
            self._owner.__dict__[relation_name] = proxy

    def remove(self, child: Union["NewBaseModel", type["NewBaseModel"]]) -> None:
        """
        Removes child Model from relation, either sets None as related model or removes
        it from the list in RelationProxy depending on relation type.

        :param child: model to remove from relation
        :type child: Model
        """
        relation_name = self.field_name
        if self._type == RelationType.PRIMARY:
            if self.related_models == child:
                self.related_models = None
                del self._owner.__dict__[relation_name]
        else:
            position = self._find_existing(child)
            if position is not None:
                self.related_models.pop(position)  # type: ignore

    def get(self) -> Optional[Union[list["Model"], "Model"]]:
        """
        Return the related model or models from RelationProxy.

        For reverse / many-to-many relations the ``RelationProxy`` is
        materialized on first read so callers always see a list-like
        return value (even when no children have been registered yet).

        :return: related model/models if set
        :rtype: Optional[Union[list[Model], Model]]
        """
        if self._to_remove:
            self._clean_related()
        if self.related_models is None and self._type in (
            RelationType.REVERSE,
            RelationType.MULTIPLE,
        ):
            return self._ensure_proxy()
        return self.related_models

    def __repr__(self) -> str:  # pragma no cover
        if self._to_remove:
            self._clean_related()
        return str(self.related_models)

def __init__(
    self,
    manager: "RelationsManager",
    type_: RelationType,
    field_name: str,
    to: type["T"],
    through: Optional[type["Model"]] = None,
) -> None:
    """
    Initialize the Relation and keep the related models either as instances of
    passed Model, or as a RelationProxy which is basically a list of models with
    some special behavior, as it exposes QuerySetProxy and allows querying the
    related models already pre filtered by parent model.

    :param manager: reference to relation manager
    :type manager: RelationsManager
    :param type_: type of the relation
    :type type_: RelationType
    :param field_name: name of the relation field
    :type field_name: str
    :param to: model to which relation leads to
    :type to: type[Model]
    :param through: model through which relation goes for m2m relations
    :type through: type[Model]
    """
    self.manager = manager
    self._owner: "Model" = manager.owner
    self._type: RelationType = type_
    self._to_remove: set = set()
    self.to: type["T"] = to
    self._through = through
    self.field_name: str = field_name
    # ``RelationProxy`` is built lazily on the first reverse/m2m use
    # (``add`` / ``get`` / ``_clean_related``) to avoid the per-model
    # allocation when the relation is never read.
    self.related_models: Optional[Union[RelationProxy, "Model"]] = None

def add(self, child: "Model") -> None:
    """
    Adds child Model to relation, either sets child as related model or adds
    it to the list in RelationProxy depending on relation type.

    For reverse / many-to-many relations the ``RelationProxy`` itself is
    stored under ``_owner.__dict__[relation_name]``, so a single O(1)
    membership check on the proxy's hash cache covers both the relation
    bookkeeping and the pydantic-visible ``__dict__`` slot — no parallel
    list, no second linear scan.

    :param child: model to add to relation
    :type child: Model
    """
    relation_name = self.field_name
    if self._type in (RelationType.PRIMARY, RelationType.THROUGH):
        self.related_models = child
        self._owner.__dict__[relation_name] = child
        return
    proxy = self._ensure_proxy()
    # ``_find_existing`` is the membership check *plus* a dead-weakref
    # probe — when a hash collision lands on a stale entry we need that
    # probe to populate ``_to_remove`` so the next ``get()`` triggers
    # ``_clean_related``.
    if self._find_existing(child) is None:
        proxy.append(child)
        self._owner.__dict__[relation_name] = proxy

class RelationsManager:
    """
    Manages relations on a Model, each Model has it's own instance.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        field_map: Optional[dict[str, "ForeignKeyField"]] = None,
        owner: Optional["Model"] = None,
    ) -> None:
        self.owner = proxy(owner)
        # ``_field_map`` lets ``_get`` build a ``Relation`` lazily by name.
        # Holding only the field reference (not a constructed Relation) is
        # what skips the per-FK Relation/RelationProxy/QuerysetProxy
        # allocation tree on every ``Model.__init__``. The map is the model's
        # ``extract_related_field_map()``, shared by all its instances, so it
        # is only read here.
        self._field_map: dict[str, "ForeignKeyField"] = (
            field_map if field_map is not None else {}
        )
        self._relations: dict[str, Relation] = dict()

    def __contains__(self, item: str) -> bool:
        """
        Checks if relation with given name is already registered.

        :param item: name of attribute
        :type item: str
        :return: result of the check
        :rtype: bool
        """
        return item in self._field_map

    def clear(self) -> None:
        for relation in self._relations.values():
            relation.clear()

    def get(self, name: str) -> Optional[Union["Model", Sequence["Model"]]]:
        """
        Returns the related model/models if relation is set.
        Actual call is delegated to Relation instance registered under relation name.

        :param name: name of the relation
        :type name: str
        :return: related model or list of related models if set
        :rtype: Optional[Union[Model, list[Model]]
        """
        relation = self._get(name)
        if relation is not None:
            return relation.get()
        return None  # pragma nocover

    @staticmethod
    def add(parent: "Model", child: "Model", field: "ForeignKeyField") -> None:
        """
        Adds relation on both sides -> meaning on both child and parent models.
        One side of the relation is always weakref proxy to avoid circular refs.

        Based on the side from which relation is added and relation name actual names
        of parent and child relations are established. The related models are registered
        on both ends.

        :param parent: parent model on which relation should be registered
        :type parent: Model
        :param child: child model to register
        :type child: Model
        :param field: field with relation definition
        :type field: ForeignKeyField
        """
        parent, child, child_name, to_name = get_relations_sides_and_names(
            field, parent, child
        )

        # print('adding parent', parent.get_name(), child.get_name(), child_name)
        parent_relation = parent._orm._get(child_name)
        if parent_relation:
            parent_relation.add(child)  # type: ignore

        # print('adding child', child.get_name(), parent.get_name(), to_name)
        child_relation = child._orm._get(to_name)
        if child_relation:
            child_relation.add(parent)

    def remove(
        self, name: str, child: Union["NewBaseModel", type["NewBaseModel"]]
    ) -> None:
        """
        Removes given child from relation with given name.
        Since you can have many relations between two models you need to pass a name
        of relation from which you want to remove the child.

        :param name: name of the relation
        :type name: str
        :param child: child to remove from relation
        :type child: Union[Model, type[Model]]
        """
        relation = self._get(name)
        if relation:
            relation.remove(child)

    @staticmethod
    def remove_parent(
        item: Union["NewBaseModel", type["NewBaseModel"]], parent: "Model", name: str
    ) -> None:
        """
        Removes given parent from relation with given name.
        Since you can have many relations between two models you need to pass a name
        of relation from which you want to remove the parent.

        :param item: model with parent registered
        :type item: Union[Model, type[Model]]
        :param parent: parent Model
        :type parent: Model
        :param name: name of the relation
        :type name: str
        """
        relation_name = item.ormar_config.model_fields[name].get_related_name()
        item._orm.remove(name, parent)
        parent._orm.remove(relation_name, item)

    def _get(self, name: str) -> Optional[Relation]:
        """
        Return the ``Relation`` for ``name``, building it on first access.

        Relations are constructed lazily so that ``Model.__init__`` does
        not allocate a ``Relation`` (and, transitively, ``RelationProxy`` /
        ``QuerysetProxy``) for every declared FK on every instance — most
        of which are never read on row-materialization paths.

        :param name: name of the relation
        :type name: str
        :return: existing or freshly constructed Relation, or None if the
            name does not correspond to a declared relation
        :rtype: ormar.relations.relation.Relation
        """
        relation = self._relations.get(name)
        if relation is not None:
            return relation
        field = self._field_map.get(name)
        if field is None:
            return None
        relation = Relation(
            manager=self,
            type_=self._get_relation_type(field),
            field_name=field.name,
            to=field.to,
            through=getattr(field, "through", None),
        )
        self._relations[name] = relation
        return relation

    def _get_relation_type(self, field: "BaseField") -> RelationType:
        """
        Returns type of the relation declared on a field.

        :param field: field with relation declaration
        :type field: BaseField
        :return: type of the relation defined on field
        :rtype: RelationType
        """
        if field.is_multi:
            return RelationType.MULTIPLE
        if field.is_through:
            return RelationType.THROUGH
        return RelationType.PRIMARY if not field.virtual else RelationType.REVERSE

def alias_for(relation_path: str) -> str:
    """
    Returns the table alias for a relation path.

    The path is the dunder separated chain of relation names from the root model
    of a single sql statement, so the alias is unique within that statement and
    stable between queries and processes. Through tables of many to many
    relations use the relation path followed by the through model name.

    :param relation_path: dunder separated relation path, empty for the root model
    :type relation_path: str
    :return: alias of the table joined under that path, empty for the root model
    :rtype: str

    if not relation_path:

:param to_field: field with relation definition :type to_field: ForeignKeyField :param parent: parent model :type parent: Model :param child: child model :type child: Model :return: parent, child, child_name, to_name :rtype: tuple["Model", "Model", str, str]

def get_relations_sides_and_names(
    to_field: ForeignKeyField, parent: "Model", child: "Model"
) -> tuple["Model", "Model", str, str]:
    """
    Determines the names of child and parent relations names, as well as
    changes one of the sides of the relation into weakref.proxy to model.

    :param to_field: field with relation definition
    :type to_field: ForeignKeyField
    :param parent: parent model
    :type parent: Model
    :param child: child model
    :type child: Model
    :return: parent, child, child_name, to_name
    :rtype: tuple["Model", "Model", str, str]
    """
    to_name = to_field.name
    child_name = to_field.get_related_name()
    if to_field.virtual:
        child_name, to_name = to_name, child_name
        child, parent = parent, proxy(child)
    else:
        child = proxy(child)
    return parent, child, child_name, to_name

@lru_cache(maxsize=2048)
def build_prefixed_columns(
    alias: str, table: sqlalchemy.Table, fields: Optional[frozenset[str]]
) -> tuple[Label[Any], ...]:
    """
    Builds labelled columns of a table, cached as labels are immutable and the
    same model/alias/fields combination is selected over and over.

    :param alias: alias of given table
    :type alias: str
    :param table: table from which fields should be aliased
    :type table: sqlalchemy.Table
    :param fields: column names (ormar aliases) to include, None for all
    :type fields: Optional[frozenset[str]]
    :return: tuple of labelled columns
    :rtype: tuple[Label[Any], ...]
    """
    alias = f"{alias}_" if alias else ""
    aliased_fields = {f"{alias}{x}" for x in fields} if fields else set()
    all_columns = (
        table.columns
        if not fields
        else [
            col
            for col in table.columns
            if col.name in fields or col.name in aliased_fields
        ]
    )
    return tuple(column.label(f"{alias}{column.name}") for column in all_columns)
